title: MammAlps aligns animal sound with video-annotated behavior
seo_description: MammAlps links wildlife audio with video-annotated behavior to evaluate visible actions, not vocal meaning.
review_depth: Targeted review of arXiv v2 sections 3.1–3.4, 5, 7.1 and 9.1–9.2; exact Zenodo v3 metadata, README, file inventory and dataset license; official CVPR Open Access indexed excerpts from the main paper and supplementary section A.1; official GitHub README, evaluation interface and LICENSE.md. The direct CVF paper and supplement fetch returned 403, so only targeted indexed excerpts were reviewed for the published version. Other supplementary methods and archive contents were not reviewed; no data or code were downloaded or run.
finding: MammAlps provides a real multimodal wildlife behavior benchmark: animal-centered video clips have matched audio and scene maps, with visible behavior labels assigned by two annotators. It evaluates observable actions and activities, not vocal meaning or animal translation.
limitations: Five wild mammal species were recorded at three sites in the Swiss National Park over six weeks; the authors withhold the exact site locations. Collection dates conflict across versions: the arXiv v2 and official CVPR main text say June–August 2023, while the arXiv/CVPR supplementary section 7.1/A.1 and Zenodo v3 say August–October 2023. The conflict persists in the published version; direct CVF fetches returned 403 and only indexed excerpts were reviewed. The period is unresolved and is not used in the atlas timeline. The published split holds out days, not verified animal identities; cross-day individual independence is unestablished. Reviewed passages describe two annotators and an unknown class but do not establish inter-annotator agreement statistics or that labeling was audio-blind. The authors acknowledge subjective behavior categories and geographic/time limits. Version 3's full data archive is 87.9 GB. Dataset terms are CC BY-NC 4.0, which excludes Talk2Nature's commercial-capable benchmark path. No audio alignment, labels, model weights, preprocessing or published result were independently reproduced.
lesson: This is a strong design comparator for testing whether sound adds predictive information beyond video, scene context and simple baselines. A behavior label is still not a message: define the prediction target, label provenance, modality ablations and grouped test before training.
next_review: Keep as a noncommercial methods reference. Before any separately approved academic reproduction, inspect the exact v3 files and dense annotations, cross-day identity structure, label reliability, event/group leakage, code and checkpoint terms, compute and storage needs. For Talk2Nature's first commercial-capable benchmark, continue seeking permissively reusable synchronized recordings with independently observed behavior labels or prepare a reviewed passive protocol.

finding: The study reports vocal babbling and repertoire development in free-ranging green-rumped parrotlet nestlings of both sexes. The paper describes a corticosterone-related repertoire difference and says the babbling repertoire was not yet integrated into functional contexts; this is developmental biology, not evidence of call translation.
limitations: One wild species and a nestling developmental stage were studied at Hato Masaguaral in Guárico, Venezuela, during 2017–2018. The current Dryad API lists version 6 with 2.56 GB of audio bouts, a 43.91 MB spreadsheet of spectrographic measurements and a 4.75 KB README; per-file sizes and SHA-256 values are recorded in the resource catalog. The study includes corticosterone supplementation, so it is not a purely passive observation dataset. The README bytes, measurement schema, individual/session joins, label provenance, audio-video synchronization, treatment groups, split design and model performance were not inspected. Dryad's current terms and policy state that published datasets are made public under CC0, and no record-specific exception is displayed; this dataset-level license evidence does not establish scientific fit, privacy/welfare suitability or model admission. lesson: Parrot vocal development is a useful research direction and can help define age-aware questions, but a changing repertoire or hormone-associated difference is not a message. title: Natural-language prompts can retrieve annotated wildlife videos
seo_description: Prompting-MammAlps tests text search over visible-behavior labels in wildlife video. It does not translate animal signals.
year_label: arXiv v1 posted July 10, 2026; official code README lists ECCV 2026
review_depth: Targeted review of arXiv v1 sections 1, 3.1–3.2, 4–7 and supplement S1.1–S1.3; official EPFL project page; pinned Hugging Face dataset card; official GitHub README, pyproject, SALMA README, repository root inventory and checkpoint issue. No dataset, code, article or model weights were acquired; no code or result was run.
finding: Prompting-MammAlps tests whether natural-language queries can retrieve camera-trap videos whose structured, visible-behavior annotations satisfy each query. The 135 ecology-informed queries include multi-attribute, multi-animal and temporal relations. This is a text interface to a video-label schema, not translation of animal signals or a two-way communication system.
limitations: The benchmark is video-only and covers seven Alpine mammal species, three sites in one Swiss national park, 15 camera views and two non-overlapping seasons (2023 and 2024); it is not a parrot or audio benchmark. The published split is by acquisition day, not verified individual identity, and cross-season distribution shift is reported. Query/video matches are built from ground-truth annotations; independent label-reliability review was not performed here. The authors report set-based F1: SALMA plus the query agent scores 0.34 across all 135 queries and 0.37 on the 113 without video-comparison prompts; zero-shot InternVideo2.0 scores 0.18 only on those 113. The commonly repeated 34% vs 18% figures therefore do not compare identical query sets. An oracle query agent on ground-truth annotations scores 0.87, so retrieval quality depends strongly on the upstream perception/annotation layer. No result was independently reproduced. Dataset terms are CC BY-NC 4.0, the code repository has no declared license, and no SALMA checkpoint release was found.
lesson: Natural-language retrieval can make an explicit behavior schema easier to explore, but it does not turn labels into an animal's message. For Talk2Nature, measure label extraction, prompt interpretation and retrieval separately; retain uncertainty, compare against simple baselines and test held-out individuals/sites before considering model training.
next_review: Keep metadata-only as a non-commercial retrieval-method comparator. Before any academic reproduction, resolve the dataset download handle, audit the exact split and label provenance, confirm code and model-weight rights, and test cross-year/site generalization. For the first Talk2Nature benchmark, continue seeking rights-cleared synchronized audio and independently timed behavior labels. AutoResearch remains NOT READY.

MammAlps-S2 contains 2,865 camera-trap video clips, 18.4 hours across 15 views, from three sites and two field seasons (2023–2024). The benchmark has 135 queries across seven mammal species, 23 actions and 12 activities; 775 videos form the test candidates.

The paper says queries were developed with a behavioral ecologist and matched to video sets using the ground-truth annotations. Exact matching excludes partial matches and retains queries with no matching video. Label reliability was not independently audited in this review.

The published split groups by acquisition day, not verified individual identity. Set-based F1 is reported per query. The 0.34 SALMA+agent result covers 135 queries; the 0.18 zero-shot InternVideo2.0 comparison covers 113 queries without video-comparison prompts. The paper also reports 0.87 for an oracle query agent applied to ground-truth annotations. None of these results was reproduced by Talk2Nature.

The dataset card declares CC BY-NC 4.0. The code repository has no GitHub license metadata or root LICENSE file; code use is unresolved. The SALMA checkpoint package was not found and a public issue asks about a future release. No dataset, code or weights were acquired.

Keep as a methods comparator for transparent retrieval over explicit labels. Do not call it animal communication, put it in a commercial-capable corpus, or treat its video-only output as audio meaning.

review_depth: Reviewed the 2017 Scientific Data article's abstract, methods, data records, Tables 3–4, technical validation, usage and rights sections; the 2016 Scientific Reports results and classification methods; the 2023 iScience abstract, dataset description, sequence-HMM methods/results, discussion and data statement; the Mendeley Data version 3 description/license and official version 1/2 and 2/3 comparisons; the Mendeley public file-list API documentation and one anonymous version 3 request (HTTP 401; documentation specifies OAuth2); the NLM catalog entry; and direct public Figshare API metadata for archive item 4556074, annotation item 4555903, FileInfo item 4555897 and Metadata.pdf item 4555900. Acquired only the 3.29 MB annotation table with verified size/MD5 for aggregate-only schema/category-count comparison, plus the 367,257-byte metadata PDF for visual review of all five pages; its source API supplies no MD5, so the receipt's SHA-256 is local provenance only. No audio/video, FileInfo.csv, code or model weights were inspected, and no published model result was reproduced.
seo_description: A bat vocalization dataset links calls to observed behavior, but it is not a translation key. Animal/session splits remain unverified.
finding: The 2017 archive describes 293,238 Egyptian fruit-bat WAV files recorded at 250 kHz and 16-bit, plus 91,080 labels derived from synchronized video, including caller, addressee, behavior and social context. The data descriptor reports a post-hoc recheck of 435 annotations, with a 4% estimated context-label error rate (95% CI 2.2–5.8%). The reviewed metadata PDF says annotation FileIDs map to FileInfo.csv; its tables describe recording-date ranges, treatment/channel settings and bats that recur across treatments, and define known, unknown and ambiguous caller/receiver codes. This makes a file/animal grouping audit plausible, but not yet verified against FileInfo rows.
limitations: The 2016 analysis reported 61% balanced accuracy for four aggressive contexts versus 25% chance, using 14,863 calls from seven adult females. Its vocalization-level cross-validation does not establish generalization to held-out bats. The 2023 follow-up used sequences from three adult females; the context HMM used 326 sequences (2,953 syllables), formed 12,900 n-grams and reported overall balanced accuracy 66 ± 10 under random eight-fold cross-validation. Shuffling syllable order left the score unchanged. These are predictions of observer-coded context, not evidence that bats or humans interpret a call as a message. The 2023 authors say behavioral experiments are needed to establish biological relevance. The laboratory archive used synchronized video, isolated chambers and specialized 250 kHz ultrasound recording; ordinary phone recordings cannot be assumed to match its bandwidth, calibration or capture conditions. The Figshare public item API declares CC0 1.0 for archive item 4556074 and lists one 3,049,199,327-byte ZIP; its payload and embedded rights notices were not inspected. The separate annotation item 4555903 declares CC0 1.0; its 3,286,405-byte file was locally size/MD5 verified. The aggregate audit found 91,080 rows, 87,986 distinct file IDs, no malformed fields and exact Table 4 count matches. These are structural/transcription checks, not independent validation. The PDF does not prove FileInfo row coverage, uniqueness or actual joins; the 31,574,701-byte FileInfo.csv was not fetched. Its API record has no upstream MD5 and the file exceeds the collector's 5 MiB per-file ceiling. Multiple annotations can belong to one file; ambiguous/unknown identities are present. No raw rows are published. No audio, video, FileInfo contents, encodings, code or weights were inspected or run.
lesson: This work offers a strong template for linking sound to independently observed context, auditing annotation uncertainty, and separating acoustic prediction from receiver comprehension. For a new benchmark, split by animal and session, keep context-only and background controls, audit duplicate calls and channels, and reserve receiver-response experiments for a separate hypothesis.
next_review: The 3.05 GB audio/video archive remains metadata-only and is not required for this bounded audit. First determine with a qualified bat-bioacoustics reviewer whether acquiring FileInfo.csv is necessary and define a bounded integrity plan for its missing upstream MD5; if justified, inspect only schema, key coverage, duplicate FileIDs, recording times/channels and links to the already audited annotation aggregate. Then test whether animal- and session-grouped splits can be formed without cross-group leakage. Keep annotations out of training unless an independently reviewed protocol and fit-for-purpose benchmark are approved. Mendeley's file-list request needs OAuth2; do not use credentials without explicit authorization. AutoResearch remains NOT READY until all project gates are met.

title: Wild parrot duet structure: sequence patterns, not decoded meaning
seo_description: Wild yellow-naped amazons show flexible duet sequences, but the study could not confidently assign meanings to calls or duets.
kind: Wild vocal-sequence study and dataset review
review_stage: Targeted primary article, dataset metadata and reuse-rights review
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher article HTML for its abstract, sites and recordings, call categorization, acoustic analyses, syntax methods and results, discussion, data-availability statement and supplementary-file inventory. Reviewed the full Dryad dataset landing page and README description and Dryad’s current reuse-rights guide. The workbook and publisher supplements were not downloaded or inspected; no published analysis was reproduced.
finding: The study examined warble duets from 13 mated pairs of wild yellow-naped amazons in north-west Costa Rica during 2006–2008. The authors report creating 1,136 duet files; 52 high-quality warble duets from 12 pairs were used in the syntax analysis. They report recurring call types, flexible ordering, 19 positive and four negative call-type associations, while most complete duet sequences were unique. This is evidence of measurable sequence structure in this study, not a translated conversation.
limitations: Analysis-specific sample counts differ: the initial lexicon is described as 469 calls from 54 duets and 13 pairs, while syntax analysis used 52 duets from 12 pairs. Methods describe 36 multi-example call types plus 11 one-time forms grouped as “Unknown”; results report 36 call types and three variants. The reported 92% repeatability came from two supervised undergraduate scorers scoring 15 hidden duets three times; it is not independent external validation. Calls could overlap and be difficult to segment, and sex assignment relied on established duet-order rules. Quadratic discriminant analysis and naive Bayes did not classify the full call-type set; pairwise naive Bayes separated only two similar types. Syntax/collocation is not semantic decoding: the authors state that they cannot confidently assign meanings to calls, collocates or duets and discuss possible territory-defense functions. Recordings used a tripod-mounted directional microphone and video, not ordinary phone capture. The species is described as Critically Endangered, so this atlas uses country-scale geography only. Dryad lists a small measurements workbook, not raw audio; the publisher separately lists a WAV and two DOCX supplements whose terms and contents were not reviewed. The specific article reuse license was not established. No Talk2Nature specialist review, independent replication or model result exists.
lesson: For Talk2Nature, represent pair or individual identity, ordered event positions, timing, overlap, uncertain caller identity and annotation provenance separately. Preserve “unknown” and distinguish a next vocal event from a response. Keep sequence structure, context association and experimentally demonstrated meaning as different evidence levels. This wild-species study is a methods comparator; it does not establish that household phone recordings are suitable or change the provisional companion-parrot pilot.
next_review: Keep this as a metadata-only methods reference, outside the first ML benchmark. Before considering the workbook, review the exact rows and pair identifiers under a specialist-led sensitive-species and research-use assessment; evaluate article and supplementary-file terms separately. A future question should test whether independent annotators can agree on call boundaries and speaker/overlap labels before comparing acoustic baselines. AutoResearch remains NOT READY.
expert_review: Not independently reviewed by a parrot bioacoustics or animal-communication specialist.
review_locator: Dahlin et al. 2026, publisher article: Abstract; Material and methods, Sites and recordings, Categorization and analysis of call types, and Duet syntax; Results, Categorization and analysis of call types and Duet syntax; Discussion; Data availability and Supporting Information. Dryad v1 landing page and README description. Dryad official reuse guidance. Workbook, WAV and DOCX files not inspected.

reuse.asset: Dryad lists README.md and Supplement_Data_DRYAD.xlsx (65.46 KB) of Raven measurements, not raw audio. The publisher lists a separate 254.5 KB WAV and two DOCX supplements.
reuse.rights: Dryad’s current reuse guide says all Dryad datasets are CC0 and recommends citation as scholarly courtesy. The specific workbook rows and any item-level notice were not inspected; no file is acquired or admitted for training. The article is marked Open Access, but its specific reuse license was not confirmed. Publisher supplements are separate artifacts with unreviewed terms.
reuse.experiment: Do not use as a model benchmark. A future specialist-reviewed exercise could test manual call-boundary, speaker and overlap agreement using permitted material, then compare sequence and acoustic baselines; keep animal/pair groups intact and separate syntax from semantic or receiver-response claims.

study_snapshot: 13 mated wild pairs in north-west Costa Rica, 2006–2008; 1,136 duet files created; the syntax analysis used 52 high-quality warble duets from 12 pairs. Directional microphone plus video.
The initial lexicon used 469 calls from 54 duets/13 pairs. Methods group 11 single-occurrence forms as Unknown alongside 36 recurring types; results report 36 types and three variants.
Reported 92% repeatability on 15 hidden duets scored three times by two supervised undergraduate researchers; scoring remained slow and overlap was difficult.
19 positive and four negative call-type associations; 47.1% of 17 analyzed types were classed as timed and 52.9% not timed. Most complete duet sequences were unique.
DFA and naive Bayes did not parse the complete call-type set; pairwise naive Bayes separated two similar call types.
Dryad v1 lists README.md and a 65.46 KB measurements workbook. Its description includes duet names and pair initials; no raw audio is listed in the deposit.
The authors report syntactic structure and explicitly say they cannot yet assign distinct semantic meanings to the calls or duets.

title: A parrot can imitate a call to address another bird. What the experiment shows.
seo_description: A controlled conure study links targeted call imitation to receiver responses; it does not establish human-like translation or justify app playback.
taxon: Orange-fronted conure (Eupsittula canicularis; the 2012 paper uses Aratinga canicularis)
review_stage: Full-text methods and results review
review_depth: Reviewed the full primary PLOS article text for the abstract, introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Ethics Statement and article license. No raw recordings, associated dataset, supplementary material or analysis code were acquired or inspected; no reanalysis was performed.
review_locator: PLOS article: Abstract; Introduction; Materials and Methods (study population, stimuli, execution and analysis); Results; Discussion; Ethics Statement; citation and copyright notice.
finding: Balsby, Momberg and Dabelsteen tested whether a call resembling one of two paired birds would selectively affect that bird. They studied 36 temporarily captive wild conures from 27 flocks. After exclusions, 44 of 72 trial periods were analyzed. Targeted birds responded with higher call rates and shorter latency overall, while some non-target responses were also recorded. The authors interpret this as evidence that vocal imitation can address a specific individual in this species and setting.
study_snapshot: 36 wild-caught orange-fronted conures from 27 flocks, placed in 18 pairs in outdoor aviaries for a short-term study.
A recorded contact-call loop was selected to resemble one of the two birds; each pair received four randomized trials.
Audio and video were used to count calls, estimate response latency and identify callers across the small social network.
44 of 72 trial periods were retained after exclusions for uncertain caller identity or outside-bird interactions.
The paper reports following Animal Behaviour Society guidelines and holding local research and CITES permits.
expert_review: This Talk2Nature synthesis has not received independent review by an avian communication specialist.
limitations: This was a controlled playback study of 36 wild-caught orange-fronted conures from 27 flocks, paired in short-term outdoor aviaries during 2007. Of 72 trial periods, 44 were retained for analysis after caller-assignment and outside-interaction exclusions. The authors report higher call rates and shorter response latency for the targeted bird overall, with a sex-specific call-rate pattern; non-target birds also responded. This supports a bounded, context-specific receiver response to acoustically targeted imitation, not decoding of sentence meaning, general conversation, or a result transferable to pet parrots, other species or phone speakers. The experiment used captured birds, repeated playback and video observation under research permits. No Talk2Nature replication or independent specialist review exists.
lesson: A receiver response can support a narrow claim about signal function in a defined context without revealing semantic content. The study also shows why a focal bird cannot always be analyzed alone: non-target flock members may respond. For our app, playback is an intervention, not a harmless conversational interface. Keep public tools passive; any later playback experiment needs qualified scientific and animal-welfare review, a defined protocol and relevant permits.
next_review: Ask a qualified avian behavior specialist to review the interpretation and welfare implications. Separately verify whether trial data, recordings or code are available and their terms before any reproduction; none were acquired in this review.

title: A 2024 model study predicts bat context—with important limits
seo_description: Caller-held-out bat context evaluation may be feasible, but exact published folds, role leakage and chamber/session effects remain unverified.
review_stage: Paper, dataset, split-feasibility and reviewer-independence review
review_depth: Reviewed all five pages of the official EUSIPCO 2024 proceedings paper and the official arXiv v1 record/manuscript, focusing on dataset filtering, evaluation protocol, model setup, metrics, class errors, data source and license. Also reviewed the first author’s linked public GitHub profile and the pinned Earth Species Library snapshot at commit 6382c52bf553569528e0a790efe16e5ae42f0094: root inventory, bat README and displayed task/split/license sections from notebooks 01, 02, 99a and 99b. No code, split files, raw media, model weights or supplements were downloaded or run. On 2026-10-23, the first author’s live GitHub owner-repository API again listed 13 public repositories (newest update 2025-10-20), and a GitHub repository search for the exact paper title returned no match. This remains a bounded search, not proof that code or splits are unavailable elsewhere. A Zenodo API search was inaccessible from this environment and is not treated as a negative result. The acquired five-page Figshare Metadata.pdf item 4555900 was visually reviewed across Tables 1–4. It lists 20 treatment periods with date ranges, group composition and channels; subject IDs, mother/date-of-birth fields; and an annotation schema with both emitter and addressee. The already-acquired 91,080-row Annotations.csv item was rechecked with an aggregate-only participant-pair audit. No raw annotation rows or IDs were exported. The 31.6 MB FileInfo.csv item and the paper’s exact fold files remain unacquired/unavailable. On 2026-10-23, the checksum-verified Annotations.csv was filtered using the paper-described context, emitter and duration rules. The aggregate-only script matches the reported 35,074-row count and summarizes file-plus-emitter and file-plus-all-known-participant group topology; it exports no row or identity values. No audio, FileInfo.csv, paper fold files, model code or model weights were acquired or run. On 2026-10-23, the official St Andrews group page was reviewed for bat vocal-communication expertise, and the TAU profile plus Nature 2025 author list were checked solely to screen fit and disclose a separate Vernes–Yovel coauthorship. No reviewer was contacted or selected. On October 24, 2026, the official Figshare API and exact CC0-declared annotation file size/MD5 were rechecked, then the aggregate audit was regenerated. The new caller-support diagnostic excludes 122 mixed-caller files and retains 99.26% of the filtered annotations; it creates no split.
review_locator: EUSIPCO 2024 paper, Sections II Dataset, III Methodology (Cross-validation, SVM and Deep learning), IV Results & Discussion, Tables I–II and confusion matrix; official arXiv v1 submission/version/license record; first author personal site and linked public GitHub repository list; Earth Species Library commit 6382c52: root file inventory, Egyptian-fruit-bat README; notebook 02 task and StratifiedKFold cells; notebook 99a license, FileInfo mapping and no-split statements; notebook 99b emitter subset selection; 2017 dataset descriptor for source context.; local aggregate report: research/figshare_bat_annotation_report.json, generated from the checksum-verified Figshare item 4555903 without exporting row values or IDs; 2026-10-23 GitHub owner-repository API inventory and exact-title repository search; St Andrews Neurogenetics of Vocal Communication group page, TAU Yossi Yovel profile, and Nature 2025 author list, reviewed only for expertise-fit and relationship disclosure
finding: Triantafyllopoulos et al. trained models to predict 11 video-coded interaction contexts from Egyptian fruit-bat calls. Their best reported result was 33.3% unweighted average recall; this predicts observed context, not message meaning or receiver comprehension. A fresh checksum-verified audit of the paper-described subset matches 35,074 annotations. Strict source-file-plus-participant graphs remain highly connected (largest 95.56%), but a role-aware caller diagnostic excluding 122 mixed-caller source files retains 34,815 annotations (99.26%) and leaves every context represented by 8–41 callers. This makes a caller-held-out test plausible for review, not validated: the paper already reports subject-independent folds, exact membership is unverified, caller identities can appear as addressees in development, and session/chamber/treatment factors remain unjoined. No split or model was created.
study_snapshot: The study reuses captive Egyptian fruit-bat ultrasound calls recorded at 250 kHz with infrared video. Context labels were manually assigned from video; 35,074 utterances remained after the stated filters.
The paper describes three subject-independent development/test folds. Within each development fold, the 70/30 train/validation split was stratified random and did not account for identity.
UAR: SVM 22.4%, ResNet-50 27.7%, EfficientNet-B0 33.3%. The paper gives 95% intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of examples, not animal/session clusters.

The best model had zero recall for grooming and often confused rare or potentially ambiguous classes. The authors discuss possible effects of class imbalance, annotation ambiguity, pup development and chamber acoustics.

The separate five-page Metadata.pdf lists 20 date-bounded treatments, social composition, channels, subject IDs and mother/date-of-birth fields. Annotation rows include emitter and addressee; negative IDs preserve a known participant pair when roles are uncertain, while zero means unknown. The full-table aggregate graph is not the paper subset or its reported folds.

The aggregate-only audit matches the paper filter count, not exact rows/folds. Strict file-plus-caller grouping yields 10 connected groups (largest 95.31%); file-plus-all-participant grouping yields 9 (largest 95.56%). Separately, excluding 122 files with multiple known callers retains 34,815/35,074 annotations (99.26%); all 11 contexts remain represented by at least eight callers. This is descriptive support, not validated folds or a split. Caller/addressee roles, exact published folds, sessions, channels, treatments and chambers remain unresolved.
expert_review: The published study is an important prior method; this Talk2Nature assessment has not received independent review by a bat bioacoustics specialist.

review_request.title: Independent methods review requested
review_request.summary: We invite an independent bat-bioacoustics or animal-behavior researcher to assess whether a caller-held-out, whole-source-file test would support a useful new-caller claim beyond the paper’s already reported subject-independent folds. The aggregate audit retains 99.26% of the filtered annotations after excluding files with multiple known callers, but it creates no split and does not hold out the same bat when it appears as an addressee in development data. Please assess role uncertainty, session/chamber/treatment effects and the exact fold evidence needed. This is a review of published context prediction, not a Talk2Nature model or claim about call meaning. Please disclose authorship of the source dataset or target result, and relevant collaborations, so independence can be characterized accurately.
questions: Would a caller-held-out, whole-source-file evaluation test generalization to new callers within this controlled cohort, given that a held-out caller could appear as an addressee in development? Which stricter grouping is needed for unseen receivers, pairs or social groups?

What evidence is needed to verify that all relevant participant roles and repeated recordings are isolated across the reported development/test folds? Which dates, channels, treatments, chambers or recording sessions could confound generalization?
Are context-only, class-prior, recording-channel/background and shuffled-label baselines adequate for this question? What uncertainty estimate respects repeated animals, pairs and sessions?
What is the smallest lawful, technically sound metadata check that could resolve the key uncertainty? Is the separate FileInfo.csv actually necessary, given its size and missing upstream checksum?

The paper reports subject-independent development/test folds, but exact membership is not verified. Would a new-caller evaluation add scientific value beyond that published result, and what smallest artifact would resolve this? Please disclose whether you authored the source dataset or 2024 prediction result, or have a relevant recent collaboration; this is used to characterize review independence, not as an automatic disqualification.
review_request.status: No independent specialist review has been received. A checksum-verified metadata audit matches the paper’s 35,074-example filter count and finds descriptive support for a caller-held-out question after excluding mixed-caller source files. No split is validated; exact published fold membership and session/chamber effects remain unresolved.

limitations: The paper’s subject-independent test split is a positive reported safeguard, but Talk2Nature has not inspected the partitions or verified which identities, roles, sessions, dates, microphones, chambers or treatments cross folds. The training/validation split inside each development set ignores identity. Confidence intervals bootstrap individual predictions rather than clustered animals or sessions. Class frequencies are unequal and grooming recall is zero. Context is an observer-coded group/action category, not a test of receiver interpretation. The 2026-10-23 public-code search covered the first author’s 13-repository owner inventory and an exact-title GitHub repository search, not coauthor/lab/archive locations; a Zenodo API search was inaccessible and yielded no negative finding. The pinned Earth Species notebook snapshot predates the EUSIPCO paper and therefore is not its promised release; a separate coauthor/lab/archive release may still exist. The repository root inventory has no visible LICENSE, and notebook 99a states code license “to be linked”; it declares dataset CC BY 4.0, which is not reconciled with Talk2Nature’s direct item-level Figshare records or derived archive-copy provenance. No independent reproduction or specialist review exists. The paper reports ImageNet-pretrained vision weights, not a bioacoustic foundation model. The arXiv v1 manuscript declares CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; proceedings-copy reuse terms were not separately reviewed. The identity graph covers the complete annotation table, not the 35,074 records used by the 2024 paper, and cannot establish whether its three folds isolate all interacting bats, emitters only, sessions, channels, treatments or chamber backgrounds. Metadata.pdf provides treatment and subject context, but the necessary per-file timestamp/channel join is in a separate 31,574,701-byte FileInfo.csv item with no upstream MD5; it was not fetched. The aggregate graph is not an independent split or leakage test. The 2026-10-24 filtered-subset audit reproduces the published row count, not the authors' exact selected-row manifest. Under source-FileID plus positive-known-participant grouping, nine components remain and the largest contains 95.56% of the filtered annotations. Under source-FileID plus positive-emitter grouping, ten components remain and the largest contains 95.31%. These strict component groupings are too concentrated for a balanced whole-component holdout. A separate caller-support diagnostic excludes 122 files with multiple known callers and retains 34,815 of 35,074 annotations (99.26%); it is descriptive support for review, not a split. It does not prevent the same animal appearing as an addressee in development data. Unknown participant roles may hide more links, and the available annotation table does not resolve session, date, channel, treatment or chamber grouping. No model was run.
lesson: The reported animal-held-out test split is a useful design target, but must be inspectable and audited by all caller/addressee identities, sessions, files, dates, channels and treatments. A 2021 archive-preparation notebook can clarify FileID-to-file joins without proving that FileInfo.csv is necessary for an unrelated later paper split audit. The Earth Species loader’s shuffled row-level split evaluates emitter identity rather than unseen-animal context prediction; the mini archive drops context labels. Compare acoustic models with class-prior, context-only and background/chamber baselines, use group-aware uncertainty, and keep prediction distinct from translation or comprehension. Because an interaction has two participant fields and uncertainty markers, a subject-independent claim should specify whether the split holds out emitters, both interacting animals, or another unit; it should also account for recording period, treatment/chamber and channel. Source tables make those checks possible in principle but do not prove the reported folds. The count-level reconstruction shows that the existing annotation table is sufficient to verify the reported filtered sample count without acquiring audio or FileInfo.csv. Strict file-plus-emitter graph components are highly imbalanced. A separate role-aware check finds descriptive support for excluding mixed-caller files, but creates no split and does not hold the same animal out when it appears as an addressee in development. An independent reviewer must decide whether this narrower estimand adds value beyond the paper's reported subject-independent folds and whether role/session/chamber effects invalidate it; otherwise defer this archive as a benchmark.
next_review: Obtain independent bat-behavior and ML/statistical review of whether a caller-held-out, whole-source-file test adds value beyond the paper's reported subject-independent folds. The aggregate support check excludes 122 mixed-caller files and retains 34,815 of 35,074 filtered annotations, but does not prevent held-out callers appearing as addressees in development or control session, channel, treatment and chamber effects. Ask which exact published fold artifact and minimum metadata join would resolve these risks; defer if no non-duplicative, defensible estimand remains. Only consider FileInfo.csv if a reviewer explains how it could change that decision; then write a bounded integrity plan before any acquisition. Keep model training and AutoResearch blocked until exact evaluation artifacts and the other readiness gates are satisfied. Before counting a review as independent, check authorship of the source dataset and target result and disclose relevant collaboration with their authors; source-author replies can clarify provenance or methods but do not satisfy independent review.

reuse.experiment: Use aggregates only for source-structure review. Any benchmark requires exact split artifacts, independently reviewed identity/session/channel grouping, artifact-specific rights, specialist review and the remaining frozen-evaluation gates.

title: BioCPPNet separates overlapping calls—it does not decode them
seo_description: A peer-reviewed bioacoustic source-separation method for macaques, dolphins and bats, with important limits on what the output means.
taxon: Rhesus macaque, bottlenose dolphin and Egyptian fruit bat
review_stage: Primary paper method/results review and pinned implementation-repository review

No code, recordings, generated mixtures, supplementary media or trained weights were acquired or executed.

finding: BioCPPNet is a supervised source-separation pipeline, an audio-cleanup step rather than a communication decoder. The study constructs mixtures by additively combining known individual vocalizations, then trains a lightweight U-Net to estimate separated waveforms. It evaluates macaque, dolphin and Egyptian-fruit-bat material. For bats, the paper reports 31,399 calls from 15 highly represented individuals, with 12 used in a closed-speaker regime and three held for an open-speaker evaluation. It reports bat validation SI-SDR 9.7 and downstream caller-identity accuracy 57.5% for the closed-speaker setting; the open-speaker SI-SDR is reported as 10.0. limitations: The mixtures are constructed from known isolated source recordings, so the reported experiment does not by itself validate performance on naturally recorded, uncontrolled field mixtures. SI-SDR and caller-identity accuracy are reconstruction proxies, not evidence that a model identified call purpose or meaning. The bat open-speaker test uses three held-out individuals from the selected subset, and Talk2Nature has not reproduced the pipeline or audited source/session overlap. The repository has no visible LICENSE at the reviewed commit, so implementation reuse is not cleared. Dataset, source audio, generated mixtures, model weights and paper terms remain separate; dolphin data are explicitly restricted. No independent reproduction or expert review exists.
lesson: Keep the analysis stages distinct: detection, overlap separation, caller/source attribution, observable context association, and experimentally supported receiver response answer different questions. Source separation could make later observation or annotation more usable, but it cannot turn an acoustic stream into a translated sentence. Any future Talk2Nature separation module needs licensed inputs, known-source synthetic fixtures, a rights-cleared model/code path and evaluation against natural field recordings before public claims.

title: Can trees talk through fungi? What mycorrhizal networks show
seo_description: Mycorrhizal networks may connect plant roots, but tree communication needs separate tests of signal transfer, receiver response and ecological effect.
review_stage: Targeted publisher-source review; not a systematic review
review_depth: Reviewed the Nature publisher record and surfaced article passages plus its author correction; the New Phytologist summary and selected discussion; and the full publisher-hosted Frontiers Opinion, including its article type and author statements. Direct rendering of the Nature article required publisher authentication in this review. The underlying studies, supplementary files and data were not reanalyzed, and no specialist review was obtained.
finding: A common mycorrhizal network describes fungal hyphae shared by roots of two or more plants; such connections have been documented in particular systems, while their prevalence and functions remain debated. Whether material moves through them, whether that movement changes a receiver, and whether information is communicated are separate questions. Karst, Jones and Hoeksema (2023) warn that popular and scientific claims about widespread forest networks and beneficial “mother tree” transfers can outrun the evidence and report positive citation bias. Henriksson et al. (2023) argue that isotope studies do not yet establish significant net carbon transfer through these networks that benefits recipients, and discuss alternative pathways. Simard, Ryan and Perry (2025) respond that multiple methods support network connections and context-dependent transfer in forests. This published disagreement is a reason to state the evidence level precisely, not to declare either that networks never occur or that trees have a demonstrated shared language.
limitations: This debate is especially about forest ecology and ectomycorrhizal systems; it does not settle every plant–fungus relationship. A fungal connection or isotope transfer is not by itself evidence that one plant sent information another received. The 2025 response is explicitly an Opinion by researchers involved in this field, not an independent replication. One author of the 2023 New Phytologist review disclosed a financial interest in an organic-fertilizer company. The linked primary studies and their methods were not exhaustively reviewed here.
lesson: Keep the claims on separate rungs: demonstrate the fungal connection; trace the material and route; measure an independent receiver response; test whether a sender-derived signal explains that response better than soil, water, root, stress or other pathways. Do not call resource movement a conversation without evidence of information transfer and receiver-specific effect.
next_review: Ask a forest mycorrhizal ecologist to review this evidence map. Then compare original tracer and network-mapping experiments, focusing on controls that distinguish hyphal connections from soil and root pathways and on independent receiver outcomes. Propose a signaling experiment only if the signal, route and receiver response can each be measured; keep this outside the acoustic AutoResearch benchmark.
expert_review: No independent forest-mycorrhizal specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature note.

reuse.experiment: No experiment, model or claim about tree-to-tree language is admitted by this note. A future study needs specialist review and controls that identify both the transfer route and an independently measured receiver response.

title: Speech models carry animal vocal patterns—not animal meanings
seo_description: A 2026 arXiv study tests whether human-speech audio encoders transfer to animal calls. It finds acoustic transfer, not animal-language translation.
taxon: Cross-species: rock hyrax, zebra finch, little owl and infant marmoset
review_stage: Full arXiv v1 HTML and version/license metadata reviewed; associated datasets, code and model assets not audited
review_depth: Reviewed the complete arXiv v1 HTML, including dataset descriptions, encoder families, caller-identification and call-type tasks, fold construction, result tables, the session-independent sensitivity analysis and conclusion. Confirmed the submitted version/date and CC BY 4.0 manuscript license on the arXiv record. No paper-linked code or data release was identified in the reviewed record/full text; this is not an exhaustive search. No audio, dataset files, code or weights were acquired or run. The arXiv record does not establish publication or peer-review status.

finding: Arias-Vergara et al. compare 15 frozen speech, speaker-verification, animal-bioacoustic and general-audio encoders on caller identification in four species and call-type classification in three. The strongest speech-pretrained representation outperforms animal-pretrained representations in three of seven task–dataset comparisons; the other four differences are not statistically significant. Controlled comparisons find no systematic advantage from multilingual coverage or animal-domain pretraining, and useful encoder layers vary with architecture. This shows that some acoustic caller and call-type information transfers across domains; the study does not predict independently observed behavior or test message meaning.
limitations: Caller-identification folds were grouped by recording session, but individuals with fewer than three sessions had their largest session split into contiguous blocks so the same caller appeared in different folds. This applied to 2/16 hyraxes, 13/33 zebra finches and all 16 little owls. The paper's session-independent sensitivity analysis reports a 0.19–0.37 UAR drop for little owls; zebra-finch UAR was 0.44 for the session-independent birds versus 0.81 for block-split birds. Therefore some caller-ID results do not estimate performance on wholly unseen individuals. The separate call-type task holds callers out, but its labels are vocal categories, not meanings. The study uses four taxa, historical source corpora and frozen encoders; fine-tuning could change the results. Source-audio, code, dependency and model-weight rights are separate and were not assessed, and results were not independently reproduced.
lesson: Human-speech pretraining can yield features useful for animal acoustic classification, but this is not the same as training an animal-language LLM. A credible Talk2Nature question would need an independently observed target, animal- and session-safe evaluation, simple acoustic and context-only baselines, and audited model/data rights. Keep acoustic identity, call type, behavior association, receiver response and meaning as distinct claims.

finding: The authors report stronger acoustic convergence at the individual than site scale in native-range Uruguay and introduced U.S. monk parakeet populations. This is evidence about acoustic identity structure and a proposed identity-signaling framework, not decoded call meaning or demonstrated receiver comprehension.
limitations: The article’s supervised random forest was trained on 156 calls from 8 known monk parakeets using 114 selected features. The reported 97.44% accuracy (95% CI 93.57–99.30) is training accuracy. The remaining 73 individual-scale calls from 9 other birds were used to produce proximity matrices and inspect clustering patterns; the paper does not report that 97.44% as held-out unseen-caller accuracy. The study reports 229 individual-scale calls and 1,353 site-scale calls. The Figshare README says its monk-parakeet selection table contains 1,596 rows, of which 1,582 were used in the paper. The pinned v1.0.0 site-scale script explains the difference: 14 site-scale calls from birds also represented in the individual-scale set are removed before the scale comparison. This source-level reconciliation was not independently recomputed from the selection CSV or WAVs. The full supplement, exact file-level rights/provenance, remaining code and dependencies were not audited. Acoustic similarity cannot by itself show what a caller intends or what a receiver understands.
lesson: For Talk2Nature, separate known-individual identification, population/site similarity, call categories, independently observed behavior, receiver response, and meaning. This is a valuable parrot-specific methods reference and a reminder to report exactly what a validation set tests. A receiver-use claim needs an appropriately reviewed behavioral experiment; the authors point to playback work for that question.

study_snapshot: At which social scale do monk-parakeet contact calls show the strongest acoustic convergence in native and introduced populations, compared with a parrot species with regional dialects?

Monk parakeets: 229 individual-scale calls from 8 native-range and 9 introduced-range individuals, plus 1,353 site-scale calls from 63 sites (37 Uruguay, 26 U.S.). Yellow-naped amazon contact calls from Costa Rica in 1994 provide a separate comparator.

Spectrographic cross-correlation and random-forest similarity; 1,844 candidate acoustic/image features were reduced to 114 for the final model. The random forest trained on 156 calls from 8 known individuals; 73 calls from 9 other individuals supported proximity/clustering analyses.

Monk-parakeet calls showed strongest convergence at the individual scale in both native and introduced ranges; the yellow-naped amazon comparison showed strongest convergence at the regional-dialect scale.
97.44% (95% CI 93.57–99.30) is reported as training classification accuracy. It is not a held-out accuracy for identifying unseen callers and does not measure call meaning.

The README reports 1,596 monk-parakeet selection rows, with 1,582 used in the paper. At pinned GitHub v1.0.0, the site-scale script identifies and removes 14 calls from birds already represented in the individual-scale sample before comparing scales. The row-level CSV/audio mapping has not been independently recomputed.
Article CC BY 4.0; Figshare item-level CC BY 4.0; GitHub code MIT; associated Zenodo archive says other-open. All dataset/code files remain metadata-only; no results independently reproduced.

title: Whombat: learn from an existing bioacoustic annotation workbench
seo_description: An experimental AOEF 1.1 export connects Talk2Nature observations to bioacoustic annotation workflows while preserving provenance and privacy limits.
year_label: Methods in Ecology and Evolution 16:19–28; version of record online 2024
review_stage: Article and guides reviewed; synthetic AOEF 1.1 export loaded with soundevent 2.10.0 and imported through Whombat 0.9.0 desktop UI; specialist review pending
review_depth: Reviewed the complete primary article through the publisher/UCL open-access record and the pinned Whombat README/license and PyPI release metadata. Read the official import, dataset, annotation-project, evaluation and installation guides. Verified the temporary Whombat 0.9.0 wheel SHA-256 against PyPI and inspected the separate Whombat GPL v3 and soundevent MIT licenses. In an isolated Python 3.12.5 environment on macOS 26.4, the exact current Listen export passed Whombat's dataset-then-project UI import. The app created one recording, two TimeInterval annotations, two notes, one task and four project tags; checksum, sample rate and duration matched, the tag table showed both sound events, and both imported creator IDs remained null. Core resolved versions were FastAPI 0.112.2, fastapi-users 12.1.3, Starlette 0.38.6 and SQLAlchemy 2.0.54. The test used only an invented WAV and a temporary SQLite database; the wheel, environment and test outputs were removed. No animal audio, participant record or model weight was tested.
finding: Whombat is a browser-based workbench for managing bioacoustic projects, reviewing recordings and human annotations, and visualizing or exchanging machine-learning predictions. The paper describes bat and avian applications. Its guide imports an AOEF dataset with an audio directory first, then its annotation project; evaluation sets and model runs are separate, and predictions are distinct from human annotations. Talk2Nature now offers an optional experimental one-way AOEF 1.1 package. The exact export imported into Whombat 0.9.0 with one recording, intervals [1, 2] and [4, 5] seconds, four visible namespaced project tags, and two notes. A missing AOEF project_tags list and a macOS canonical-path issue were identified and fixed/documented during this synthetic compatibility test.
limitations: This is annotation and model-assisted review infrastructure, not a decoder of animal intent or a general animal-language translator. The app-level check establishes format interoperability only for Whombat 0.9.0 and the recorded test stack; other dependency versions, mobile behavior, real recordings, label quality and research suitability remain unverified. The test used invented audio only. Full Talk2Nature IDs, declared animal context and any Station journal stay in an unencrypted provenance sidecar; inspect it before sharing. Whombat's path check requires one canonical absolute audio-root path; on macOS /tmp may resolve to /private/tmp. No reverse import exists, and the sidecar is still the source of truth. The Whombat v0.9.0 code is GPL v3; the soundevent library is MIT; the article is CC BY 4.0. These licenses cover separate assets.
lesson: Do not build a second full research annotation editor before proving a distinct user need. Keep the novice field companion focused on bounded observation and local review; investigate an optional research-workbench exchange path, with model suggestions preserved separately from accepted human labels.
next_review: Have an independent bioacoustics or research-software specialist review the AOEF field mapping before recommending it for a study. Consider other Whombat/dependency versions only in a fresh synthetic test. Keep the feature experimental; real recordings, participant intake and model-training admission require separate rights, consent, privacy and scientific-protocol gates.

title: ANIMAL-SPOT: parrot call detection is not translation
seo_description: ANIMAL-SPOT reports parrot sound detection and monk-parakeet call classification. Those outputs identify acoustic classes, not what an animal means.
review_stage: Full main-article text and split methods reviewed; current repository access terms and API field semantics rechecked but not accepted; supplement, archive contents and specialist review remain open
review_depth: Read the full publisher article text, including the target/noise and call-type methods, preprocessing, split policy, results, discussion and ethics/data-collection description, alongside Tables 1 and 3 from the earlier targeted full-text review. The paper states that samples from one recording stay in only one split, with a default 70/15/15 train/validation/test split; it does not establish individual-animal holdout. It reports mean 97.9% test-set accuracy (range 94.5–99.8%) and, separately, 95.9% average AUC (range 91.7–99.1%) across 33 additional unseen animal-specific recordings. Monk-parakeet call-type accuracy is 92.7% on human-labeled test samples and 88.4% on detector-selected segments. Re-read Edmond V2.0 API metadata on October 23, 2026: file restricted=false, fileAccessRequest=true, dataset-level CC BY 4.0 and the same provider MD5. The official Dataverse 6.11 API documentation says access-request settings are ignored when a file is unrestricted. Edmond's own download guide separately requires acceptance of its terms and dataset license; the current Terms' MPS-associated service wording still does not explicitly clarify its application to external downloaders of existing public datasets. The supplement's split tables, exact V2 archive manifest and individual/session recurrence remain unreviewed. No data, code or model was acquired or run; no terms were accepted and metrics were not reproduced.
finding: ANIMAL-SPOT is a staged, species-specific acoustic detection/classification framework, not one zero-shot animal-language model. Its paper reports recording-level partitioning (samples from a recording stay within one split) and a default 70/15/15 train/validation/test split. For target/noise detection, it reports mean test-set accuracy of 97.9% (range 94.5–99.8%) and, separately, an average AUC of 95.9% (range 91.7–99.1%) across 33 additional unseen animal-specific recordings. In a separate monk-parakeet task, the paper reports 92.7% call-type accuracy on human-labeled test samples and 88.4% on detector-selected segments. These are upstream-reported results, not Talk2Nature measurements; acoustic class prediction does not establish behavior, receiver comprehension or meaning.
limitations: The recording-level split supports a held-out-recording interpretation, but the article does not state that individual animals are held out; the repository's YEAR+TAPENAME grouping guidance also does not prove individual separation. Edmond metadata lists one public 547,403,503-byte V2.0 archive, but its internal contents and split files remain unreviewed, and the deposit is described as target/noise data rather than the paper's separate call-type corpus. The API's fileAccessRequest=true flag is not itself an access-request gate because the file is marked restricted=false; official Dataverse documentation says the flag is ignored for unrestricted files. Edmond separately requires acceptance of its terms and the dataset license for downloading, and the current Terms of Use does not separately explain the external-downloader scope; no terms were accepted. Metrics and supplementary split tables were not reproduced or independently checked. The work does not show one zero-shot model that translates across species, and it is not evidence of companion-parrot or phone-microphone performance.
lesson: For an app, treat any future detector or call-type output as a reviewable hypothesis and keep it separate from what the person observed. A staged detector can help find candidate sounds; it cannot answer what the animal is communicating.
next_review: Candidate question: can the published monk-parakeet target/noise baseline be reproduced on the exact V2.0 archive using its recording-held-out split, with performance reported per held-out recording? The public API metadata has clarified that fileAccessRequest=true does not gate this unrestricted file, but it has not clarified Edmond's separate terms of use for an external researcher. Before any reproduction, resolve whether those terms permit Talk2Nature's intended external use; accepting terms or retrieving files requires explicit owner approval. If cleared, inspect archive and split manifests, verify label provenance and check whether animal identities recur across recordings, then ask a qualified bioacoustics reviewer whether the data and metrics answer a useful detection question. Add an animal-held-out claim only if identity metadata and an approved split support it. Until these gates pass, keep the record metadata-only and AutoResearch NOT READY.
expert_review: Not independently reviewed by a parrot-communication or bioacoustics specialist.

title: CoarseSoundNet: soundscape context, not animal language
seo_description: CoarseSoundNet classifies broad animal, human and environmental soundscape layers; it does not identify a species or decode animal meaning.
year_label: arXiv v2 posted May 21, 2026; paper described as under review in the pinned code-repository README checked October 13, 2026
review_stage: Full preprint review and official code/model/dataset metadata inspection; no independent reproduction
review_depth: Reviewed the full arXiv v2 HTML: data composition, model comparison, transfer to BEsound, silence handling, threshold/duration post-processing, error analysis and ecological-index case study. Reviewed the pinned GitHub repository/README/license, Hugging Face revision and file/rights metadata, and the Zenodo record plus read-only API metadata. No code, model weights, dataset archive, audio, figures or supplementary files were downloaded or run.
finding: CoarseSoundNet targets broad, potentially co-occurring soundscape layers: anthropophony (human-made sounds), biophony (animal sounds), geophony (natural abiotic sounds) and an explicitly handled silence condition. The manuscript reports strong EDANSA-2019 test performance but a marked drop on the different BEsound recording domain, especially for human and geophysical sounds. Its best BEsound macro-F1 of 0.799 applies class-specific thresholds and window-count settings selected on BEsound itself; it should be treated as a tuned evaluation result rather than an untouched holdout estimate. The ecological case study uses model predictions to pre-filter audio before calculating conventional acoustic indices. This can help characterize recording context, but it does not say which species vocalized or what a call means. The paper uses public EDANSA together with BEsound and other collections that are not all directly accessible. Code, weights, article and data have distinct licenses: the pinned training repository declares MIT, the Hub model declares CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the arXiv paper declares CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and Zenodo's API declares CC BY 4.0 for the EDANSA record while the rendered license field is blank.
limitations: The paper remains a preprint in the records reviewed: the author-group GitHub README says it is under review, and an author's publication list places it under preprints; a peer-reviewed version was not verified. The BEsound evaluation data also informed selection of post-processing thresholds/counts, which limits the interpretation of the best reported score as independent generalization. Domain, recorder and annotation differences matter; reported errors include insect sounds confused with biophony, wind/background noise around silence/geophony, and masking when classes co-occur. Some training collections are private or available only on request. The code repository is marked under construction. Model weight reuse is non-commercial under its declared CC BY-NC-SA terms; underlying encoder, dependencies and all dataset components need separate review. No Talk2Nature result is reproduced.
lesson: This is a useful context-layer reference for later ecological analysis, not a conversation system. Keep any eventual app context optional, human-reviewed and multi-label; preserve co-occurrence and unknowns, and do not silently convert broad soundscape predictions into a focal animal identity or behavioral explanation. For model evaluation, never tune thresholds or window-count rules on the same set presented as an untouched test result. The current Field Companion remains a passive, user-led observation tool; this evidence does not justify adding an automatic prediction feature.
next_review: After a peer-reviewed version or independent review is available, compare its evaluation protocol with Talk2Nature's leakage-safe benchmark checklist. Ask an ecoacoustics reviewer whether one narrow context-label task would help the existing human annotation workflow. Before any acquisition or model run, resolve exact EDANSA license display and file/label provenance, review all component rights, define grouped splits and freeze the test set. Keep AutoResearch NOT READY.

title: WhAM: acoustic style transfer is not whale translation
seo_description: WhAM generates sperm-whale-style audio and learns features for coda classification. Its acoustic style transfer does not translate whale meaning.
year_label: arXiv v1 posted 2025-12-01; official project repository identifies the work as NeurIPS 2025
review_stage: Full main-text review and targeted methods/artifact metadata review; no independent reproduction
review_depth: Read the full arXiv v1 main text from abstract through limitations, and reviewed targeted Appendix E sections on training data, compute, downstream classification and expert perceptual evaluation. Checked the official repository README/license and pinned source revision, the DSWP dataset card and its current repository revision, and the Zenodo model-weight record. No code, audio, datasets, model weights, paper figures or supplementary files were downloaded or run; Appendix D and artifact contents were not fully audited.
finding: WhAM fine-tunes the music-pretrained VampNet masked acoustic token model in two stages: domain adaptation on animal-audio collections, then sperm-whale-specific training on DSWP and CETI. The paper describes 2,507 DSWP and 7,653 CETI annotated codas for this work. It evaluates generated audio with Fréchet Audio Distance and a five-expert listening study, and tests learned embeddings on coda detection, rhythm, social-unit and vowel-type classification. The paper explicitly defines “translation” as converting prompts, including noise or other animal sounds, into sperm-whale coda-like acoustic style; it says semantic translation remains a separate, more ambitious goal. On the reported classification table, WhAM exceeds simple random/majority baselines but the reported specialist or general bioacoustic embeddings perform better across these tasks. For example, social-unit accuracy is 70.5% for WhAM versus 93.2% for BirdNET. The paper describes social-unit classification within data from a single vocal clan as closer to speaker identification than dialect classification.
limitations: The downstream protocol describes an 80/20 label-stratified train/test split and selects the best classifier checkpoint based on test-set performance. The reviewed description does not establish a separate validation set or grouping by whale, recording, session or source, so the reported test metrics should not be treated as an untouched independent estimate. The public DSWP card currently lists 1,501 isolated snippets (~45 minutes; 585 MB), fewer than the paper’s 2,507 DSWP training codas; the exact relationship is unresolved. The card says the clips lack behavioral context and per-file recording-system metadata and all come from one clan and region. The paper identifies codec limitations, unnatural synthetic click onset/decay/background, echolocation-like artifacts and possible echolocation contamination in data prepared as communication codas. Its expert study involved five specialists with only moderate inter-expert agreement. The acoustic outputs and classification labels do not demonstrate receiver comprehension, behavioral function or meaning. The paper is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, code MIT, DSWP card CC BY 4.0, while the weight record displays no license; these are distinct component rights. No independent reproduction or specialist review occurred.
lesson: Use WhAM to study a specific generative-modeling and representation-learning approach, not as a conversation engine or a reason to play generated animal-like sounds to animals. Its test-set model selection and unspecified entity grouping are concrete examples for Talk2Nature’s benchmark rules: group correlated samples before splitting, freeze an untouched test set, select checkpoints only on validation data, compare simple and domain-specific baselines, and keep acoustic similarity separate from biological function or meaning.
next_review: If this becomes relevant to a future benchmark, first obtain qualified cetacean-bioacoustics review, resolve exact DSWP/CETI release provenance and rights, verify a grouped split by relevant animal/recording/session, and freeze validation and test protocols before any model evaluation. Resolve the model-weight license and dependency/data terms before download or execution. Do not use it in the public companion or initiate playback. AutoResearch remains NOT READY.
expert_review: No independent cetacean-bioacoustics specialist review, author verification or Talk2Nature reproduction has occurred.

Audubon Core describes biodiversity-related multimedia resources and offers terms for aspects such as rights and access. Issue #759 is closed, and its visible discussion says guide section 3.4 already states the field-descriptor rule; the official review index was stale. Darwin Core distinguishes an organism, an occurrence and a media entity; a generic sound candidate or observer note should not be promoted to a confirmed occurrence. No mapping of current Station or Listen fields has been validated. Current device time is declared unverified, exact location is not collected, and rights for the standard-document text were not established. The observed versioned-URL failures are environment-specific; the pre-review GitHub snapshot is not evidence of final published schemas.

Before drafting an adapter, define what one sampling event means and retrieve the official schemas; map only fields with a verified equivalent, preserve provenance and unknowns, distinguish media from observations and identifications, report information loss, and validate against a pinned official profile. title: How great tits respond to a distant species’ mobbing calls
seo_description: A 2025 playback study tests great-tit responses to Carolina wren mobbing calls, with limits on what receiver behavior proves about meaning.
review_stage: Publisher-indexed methods/results and institutional abstract reviewed; no article file, data, or independent specialist review
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher-indexed Methods, Results and Discussion passages and the University of Western Australia repository abstract and publication/license metadata. The publisher states 96 wild great tits, six playback treatments with 16 birds each, and a single playback per bird. The indexed text exposes stimulus construction and behavioral outcomes; direct ScienceDirect retrieval returned HTTP 403, so figures, supplements, full statistical details, and article-level context were not reviewed.
finding: Great tits approached the loudspeaker more often during call playbacks than during control playbacks, but approach did not significantly differ among call treatments. Wing-flicking was more likely after the complete two-part call sequence (labelled FME–D by the authors) than after D-only calls or controls for both great-tit and Carolina-wren stimuli. The study reports no significant difference between the two species’ sequence treatments (P=0.12; wide confidence interval), so it does not establish their equivalence.
limitations: This is one field playback study of European great tits responding to unfamiliar Carolina wren calls, not a test of arbitrary call combinations or open-ended communication. The authors note that the alert/recruitment functions of the Carolina wren's FME and D parts were not confirmed. It did not include reversed-order Carolina-wren sequences, so it does not isolate call order as the cause. Carolina-wren stimuli came from four recorded individuals but were reduced to two constructed tracks per call treatment; the authors note that more stimulus diversity would be ideal. Similar behavior can reflect response to a mobbing-like acoustic pattern without demonstrating a shared semantic representation or receiver translation. No Talk2Nature model or app feature was tested.
lesson: Treat receiver actions as the measured outcome. To test how a sequence is decoded, compare sequence and component calls, reverse order, control acoustic similarity and novelty, use diverse independent callers, and predefine a receiver-side behavioral measure. Cross-species response is a hypothesis-generating bridge, not evidence of unrestricted shared language.
next_review: Review the full article and any trial-level data through an accessible lawful route; verify data availability and exact article terms; then ask an independent avian-communication specialist to assess whether the design distinguishes sequence structure from shared acoustic cues. Do not add animal-directed playback to the Field Companion.

Background noise, southern house-wren song, Carolina-wren D, Carolina-wren FME–D, great-tit D, and great-tit FME–D.
Sixteen great-tit FME–D tracks used one donor individual each. Carolina-wren stimuli drew on four recorded birds but used two constructed tracks per call treatment.

Approach distinguished call from control playbacks, not the call treatments from one another. Wing-flicking was higher after sequence than D/control playbacks; great-tit and Carolina-wren sequence responses did not significantly differ.
No reversed Carolina-wren sequence was tested. The response is behavioral evidence about this playback context, not a translation or general semantic result.
