title: Common endophyte networks: resource transfer is not communication
seo_description: A 2026 controlled study reports isotope transfer through common endophyte networks; it does not test plant-to-plant messages or signal interpretation.
year_label: Published 8 June 2026; version of record 20 August 2026
review_stage: Full primary article and repository metadata reviewed; no artifact reproduction or independent specialist review
review_depth: Full publisher article reviewed: abstract, introduction, results, materials and methods, statistical analysis, data-availability statement, limitations and rights. Official GitLab project metadata, current main commit, root tree and per-file metadata were checked; no dataset bytes, R code, README or supplementary file was retrieved or run.
finding: In split-plate laboratory experiments with Arabidopsis thaliana, Waschk et al. report that three tested endophytes formed common endophyte networks and moved some isotope-labelled resources from donor-side soil into receiver plant tissues. The paper reports 55% higher amino-acid-derived 15N in receiver plants for Fusarium temperatum and a smaller 13C enrichment for Trichoderma viride (+2.83% over control); it also reports 38% greater plant biomass for F. temperatum in this setup. These are bounded physiological and isotope outcomes, not a decoded signal or a demonstrated plant conversation.
limitations: The experiment used a controlled split-Petri-dish system, Arabidopsis hosts and three fungal endophytes, not a forest or natural field network. The design lacked a no-donor treatment and some no-receiver isotope controls; the authors could not distinguish direct hyphal 15N delivery from fungal exudate or necromass entering receiver soil. Deuterium appeared in plant isotope controls, indicating an abiotic transfer pathway. The paper says natural-system CEN involvement remains untested. It measured resource enrichment and plant physiology, not a sender-derived information signal, receiver behavior or interpretation; resource transfer cannot establish plant-to-plant communication. CENs are distinct from common mycorrhizal networks, so this study does not settle the forest mother-tree debate. The linked data and code have no declared license in the reviewed repository metadata and were not inspected.
lesson: Keep fungal connection, isotope movement, plant physiological response, information transfer and receiver interpretation as separate claims. A measurable transfer route is not by itself a communication signal. Any claim about signaling needs a specified signal, controlled route, sender-side change and independent receiver response with alternatives tested.
next_review: Ask a qualified plant–fungus ecologist to review the split-plate controls and interpretation. Separately establish exact data and code terms, contents and reproducibility before any artifact acquisition or run. Keep this as a non-acoustic methods reference, outside the current animal-audio benchmark and mobile-sensing capability.
expert_review: No independent plant–fungus specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature note.
review_locator: Nature Scientific Reports 16, article 26111: Abstract; Results; Study limitations; Materials and Methods; Data availability; Rights and permissions. GitLab project API, main tree and file metadata at commit 5b4ea51c038213e62feb6580daa5a48ccbfa32ff. Checked 2026-10-13.
study_snapshot: Arabidopsis thaliana donor and receiver plants in a controlled split-Petri-dish setup; three endophytes tested separately: Trichoderma viride, Mucor hiemalis and Fusarium temperatum.
Six plates per endophyte and isotope treatment for donor–receiver trials; four no-receiver plates per species; five isotope-control replicates per treatment; ten natural-abundance controls.
15N-labelled amino acids and ammonium, 13C-labelled amino acids, and deuterated water.
F. temperatum increased receiver-plant amino-acid-derived 15N by 55% and biomass by 38%; T. viride increased receiver-plant 13C by 2.83% over control. 15N-ammonium transfer was not detected.
Some receiver isotope enrichment supports a bounded resource-transfer result; several transfer routes remain ambiguous, and communication or receiver understanding was not tested.

atlas.location_note: Controlled laboratory study with no field collection or reported study-site location; author affiliations are not used as collection sites.

title: Lilac-crowned Amazon calls vary with context; meaning remains a question
seo_description: A 2016 Lilac-crowned Amazon study links call-note patterns with nine observed contexts; it does not decode call meaning or validate a context-prediction model.
review_stage: Full-text primary-source review
review_depth: Reviewed the full publisher article for abstract, field methods, context definitions, acoustic measurements, statistical analyses, results, discussion, data availability, ethics and rights; reviewed the additional-file inventory. The research viewer failed or timed out on selected binary supplements. No article assets, audio, data or code were downloaded, opened, executed or redistributed; no independent reanalysis or specialist review was performed.
review_locator: Frontiers in Zoology 13:40 (2016): Abstract; Methods—Vocal recording, Vocal analyses, Statistical analyses; Results—design characteristics and classification by note-type; Discussion; Availability of data and materials; Ethics approval and consent; Additional files; Rights and permissions.
finding: Montes-Medina, Salinas-Melgoza and Renton analyzed 75 hours of non-continuous field recordings from 61 free-living Lilac-crowned Amazons. They report 8,622 notes classified into 152 note-types; after excluding single-occurrence types, 8,571 notes formed 101 note-types emitted at least twice. The researchers associated calls with nine behavioral contexts, and common note-types occurred in several contexts with different proportions. Context was associated with acoustic features and note-type frequency. Separately, a nested permuted discriminant analysis distinguished 28 note-types while accounting for repeated notes from individuals (46.9% observed classification versus 9.6% expected under the paper's permutation null, P=0.001). That is note-type discrimination, not prediction of behavior from sound and not evidence that calls have human-language meanings.
study_snapshot: 61 free-living Lilac-crowned Amazons (Amazona finschi), identified at nest sites or inferred as potentially distinct individuals from recording day and distance for some off-site contexts.
75 hours of non-continuous recordings made at about 30 m with directional microphones and solid-state recorders; 44.1 or 48 kHz WAV, with 48 kHz material resampled to 44.1 kHz.
Nesting, threat, alarm, foraging, perched, take-off, flight, landing and food soliciting. The study is observational; it did not test playback responses.

Researchers classified 8,622 notes into 152 note-types. Acoustic-parameter analyses used 58 types meeting frequency and recording-quality criteria; the note-type pDFA used 28 types emitted by more than one individual.

Publisher lists a 116 kB XLSX of statistical-analysis data, context descriptions, a note-frequency table and sound examples. Article text is CC BY 4.0; the publisher says data made available with the article are CC0 unless otherwise stated. Supplement binaries and any file-specific exceptions were not checked.
limitations: This is a single-species field study with non-continuous recordings and researcher-assigned behavioral contexts, not a validated context classifier or modern ML benchmark. The article notes low sample sizes in some contexts and says playback evidence is needed to establish signal function. GLMM analyses excluded food soliciting; the pDFA classifies note types, not behavioral contexts, and its permutation comparison is not an untouched held-out-animal test. Some off-nest individual identities were inferred from day and distance. The paper does not report quantified independent context-label agreement. Supplement descriptions conflict with several linked file extensions; no data or example audio was opened, and the listed files do not describe a full 75-hour archive. The acoustic setup and wild species do not validate ordinary phone capture or household-parrot behavior.
lesson: Keep the observation, acoustic event, behavioral context and interpretation as separate records. A call can be associated with multiple contexts, and a note-type classification result is not a behavior prediction or translation. Use this paper to design labels and confound checks, not as evidence that Talk2Nature can infer a call's meaning.
next_review: Ask an independent avian-bioacoustics reviewer to assess the context definitions, individual assignment and nested pDFA. If a concrete reproduction need emerges, first retrieve the exact XLSX and supplement inventory through an authorized route, inspect columns and provenance, resolve the publisher's file-type mismatches, and verify the CC0 notice for each selected data file. Do not train or treat the sample sounds as a benchmark.
expert_review: This Talk2Nature synthesis has not been independently reviewed by an avian-bioacoustics specialist.

title: Phones can record wildlife, but they are not interchangeable sensors
seo_description: Nightingale and bat field studies show where smartphone recordings can help—and why microphone models, call ranges and field validation matter.
taxon: Multiple taxa: common nightingale and bats
review_stage: Selected full-text methods, results, discussion, data-availability and rights review
review_depth: For Jäckel et al. (2021), reviewed the PLOS paper's methods, citizen-recording quality results, device playback comparison, discussion, rights and Zenodo data statement; the cited Zenodo deposit remains unreviewed. For Gili et al. (2024), reviewed the full publisher article and the March 13, 2024 Dryad record, visible file list and embedded README structure, as well as Dryad's CC0 and responsible-sharing policies. The separate README download returned HTTP 403. No audio archive, article supplement or code was acquired or reproduced, and no independent specialist review was completed.
finding: Two different studies show that smartphones can support bounded wildlife-acoustic tasks, but they do not create a uniform sensor. Jäckel et al. compared 5,679 Berlin citizen-science nightingale recordings with expert recordings: 53% of citizen recordings were categorized as complete songs versus 100% of expert recordings, and signal-to-noise ratios were lower for citizen recordings. In a small controlled playback comparison, estimated frequency limits varied by device. The authors nevertheless considered the citizen recordings useful for questions based on relative song-type occurrence, while cautioning about exact acoustic measurements. Gili et al. tested built-in microphones for selected 8–24 kHz bat calls. Their field/pilot work covered 35 phone models and nine bat species, but found device-model variation, occasional aliasing and loss of calls near the upper detection limit; the authors recommend preliminary detectability checks and expert verification of at least some identifications.
limitations: These studies cover different species, frequency ranges, devices, apps, protocols and outcomes; their results cannot be pooled into a general phone-quality score. The nightingale work is a Berlin project and its controlled device set was small. The bat work focuses on selected calls within 8–24 kHz at Italian and Spanish sites; it does not establish general ultrasonic capture above that range. Neither study validates current phones, current operating systems, browser capture or Talk2Nature's exact audio path. Acoustic recording or species-level detection does not demonstrate receiver comprehension or call meaning.
lesson: Keep the phone as an accessible observation tool, but treat device and capture path as part of the measurement. A browser level check is not microphone calibration, and a WAV export does not make recordings comparable across phones. Any later scientific protocol should test the chosen phone models and app path against a reference recorder for the target species and frequency range, then preserve the untouched source and protocol metadata. Collect only the minimum device information needed, with consent; do not fingerprint participants. Keep detection, identification, behavior association and meaning as separate claims.
next_review: Ask an independent bioacoustics/mobile-audio reviewer to define a small, no-animal device-characterization protocol for the exact Android and iOS capture paths: paired phone/reference recordings, target frequency ranges, browser audio processing, device/session grouping, and pass/fail limits. For the Dryad bat deposit, review the 17.46 MB Appendix S6 examples only if a concrete research question justifies it, with a recorded checksum and file-level privacy/location screen; defer the 3.89 GB archive. The linked Zenodo nightingale deposit remains unreviewed. Keep participant intake closed until protocol, consent, privacy, rights and withdrawal gates are approved.

review_request.title: Independent review of smartphone recording checks
review_request.summary: We invite bioacoustics, acoustic-measurement or mobile-audio specialists to assess whether a small, no-animal reference test of device and app-path variation would answer a useful question without overstating microphone calibration or field suitability. This is a critique of a possible next step; no test protocol, pass/fail threshold or device recommendation has been approved.
questions: Would a no-animal reference test answer a useful prerequisite question for a defined acoustic task, or is it too detached from field conditions to guide the app?
Which capture paths should be compared first, and what source/reference recording would separate microphone, operating-system/browser processing and app settings?
What minimum device/session metadata supports reproduction without collecting serial numbers, account identifiers, precise locations or persistent device fingerprints?
Which measurements and uncertainty summaries matter for a selected frequency range, and is any pass/fail threshold defensible?
What can the app's short input-level check honestly tell a visitor, and what result would change the decision to build a more advanced device-check workflow?
review_request.status: No independent specialist review has been received; no bench protocol, pass/fail threshold or device recommendation is approved, and no physical-device test is claimed.

expert_review: No independent bioacoustics or mobile-audio specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature synthesis or proposed device protocol.
review_locator: Jäckel et al. 2021, PLOS ONE 16(6):e0253763: Materials and methods; citizen-science recording-quality results; device playback test; Discussion; data availability and rights. Gili et al. 2024, Biodiversity and Conservation 33:1623–1643: mobile-device protocol; results; Discussion; data availability and rights. Checked 2026-10-13.
study_snapshot: Citizen scientists used the Naturblick app; 5,679 recordings from Berlin in 2019 were compared with expert recordings. Recording instructions were intentionally limited, so the sample also reflects varied user behavior and context.

53% of citizen-science recordings versus 100% of expert recordings were classified as complete songs. Citizen recordings had lower signal-to-noise ratios; frequency estimates varied among devices in the small playback comparison.

Selected built-in phone microphones were compared with a reference bat detector for calls in an 8–24 kHz range. The paper reports model-level differences and calls near the upper limit were more likely to become undetectable with distance.

The pilot tested 35 phone models across 80 volunteer sessions and reported nine recorded species; some recordings remained unidentified and five tested models showed aliasing artifacts. The authors recommend preliminary device checks and expert validation.

The versioned Dryad page lists an Appendix S6 examples archive (17.46 MB), a full mobile-recordings archive (3.89 GB), and a 6.49 KB README. Its embedded README describes 80 sessions with device model, operating system, date, species folders and site-code-to-municipality mappings. Dryad's current guidance says hosted datasets are CC0 1.0; the item page itself shows no record-specific license. The README download returned HTTP 403 and no audio was acquired.

CC0 per Dryad policy supports reuse, but metadata review does not establish archive contents, label quality, location masking, consent scope or benchmark fitness. Keep the record metadata-only; if justified, inspect the smaller examples archive first under a documented protocol.

Make phone variability visible before recording. The existing eight-second check measures temporary browser input only; it does not calibrate microphones or establish species coverage. Preserve a simple local observation path while reserving comparative scientific claims for a reviewed device protocol.

atlas.location_note: This synthesis combines distinct field studies in Berlin, Northern Italy and Seville; no single point represents the evidence or validates global phone performance.

title: Strong bird-call labels can test detectors, not communication
seo_description: PteroSet v5 labels bird calls for detection, but its time-lapse data, two-landscape split and lack of behavior labels do not test communication.
review_stage: Full preprint methods and evaluation; versioned dataset manifest and header-only metadata schema; pinned code review
review_depth: Reviewed arXiv v2 methods, annotation design, dataset schema, technical validation, project-split evaluation, discussion and license; the exact Zenodo v5 API manifest; and pinned repository source. All 12 provider-reported filenames, byte sizes and MD5 strings match this catalog; no dataset file bytes were hashed. A 4,096-byte HTTP 206 range of metadata_v2.csv was streamed transiently and only its header line inspected; it names location_id, recorder_id, date_recorded, latitude and longitude. Raw GitHub source files were fetched read-only into a transient filter for static review; none were saved to the project, installed or executed. No data-row values were reviewed or saved; no annotation rows, manifest rows, audio or checkpoints were inspected. No independent reproduction or specialist review occurred.
finding: PteroSet v5 is a useful time-frequency bird-event detection comparator: its released record describes 563 time-lapse WAVs totaling 73.62 hours, 15,372 expert annotations and 6,702 species-level determinations across 168 species. It offers a binary bird-presence baseline. That target is whether a window overlaps an annotated bird vocalization, not what a bird is communicating. The dataset supplies no independently observed behavior, interaction, recipient response or communicative-meaning labels.
limitations: The five reported projects cover two named landscapes: MAP1 at Pivijay, Magdalena, and PPA1–PPA4 at Puerto Asís, Putumayo. Therefore only the MAP1 test fold holds out a distinct named landscape; the four PPA folds test other projects while the same broad landscape remains in training. This is an audit inference from the paper's project/site table, not a reanalysis. Each time-lapse file concatenates 10-second clips sampled 30 minutes apart; its timeline is discontinuous, and the v5 segment manifest is needed to recover original segment mapping. Annotators retained clearly identifiable signals and excluded faint or ambiguous calls. The paper labels windows with no overlapping annotation as negative, which should not be equated automatically with confirmed biological silence. The pinned code declares Zenodo record 21829388 and its README lists metadata_v2.csv and segment_manifest.csv. All 12 names, sizes and provider MD5 strings in the exact v5 API manifest match this catalog, but no file bytes were hashed. A bounded 4,096-byte HTTP 206 range request streamed metadata_v2.csv; only the header was inspected, confirming location_id, recorder_id, date_recorded, latitude and longitude fields. Row values were not reviewed or saved. The README downloader resolves the concept DOI's latest version by default, and its manifest example still names metadata.csv. The pinned data_reader.py has a breakpoint() in initialization and emits latitude/longitude into annotation records. Treat code-to-file compatibility, data joins and location sensitivity as unresolved; precise wildlife coordinates require a documented handling decision before any reuse or public mapping.
lesson: Use event detection and species identification as bounded tool functions that can help a person review sound. Preserve continuous-sample boundaries, source-recording groups, site and season when designing splits. A detector score is not context, intent, or a conversation; any later meaning claim needs independent behavior and receiver-response evidence.
next_review: Before a detection-only reproduction, obtain independent bioacoustics review of whether this question is useful and how precise location fields should be handled. The exact v5 API names, byte sizes and provider MD5 strings now match the catalog, and a header-only metadata_v2.csv range confirms that the schema includes recorder, date and coordinate fields; no file bytes were hashed and row values were not reviewed or saved. The reader pins record 21829388 but the downloader still resolves the concept DOI's latest release by default; the README example still names metadata.csv, and data_reader.py retains an interactive breakpoint() and writes coordinates into annotation output. Resolve those issues only in a separately reviewed, version-pinned workflow; inspect annotation/manifest joins only if an explicit purpose and location protocol justify it. Then freeze a grouped, non-overlapping test protocol. Keep dataset, code and model weights metadata-only until their separate gates pass; AutoResearch remains NOT READY for the communication/context objective.
expert_review: No independent bioacoustics or machine-learning specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature assessment.
review_locator: Ruiz et al., arXiv:2605.20578v2 (2026): data collection; annotation; data records; technical validation; cross-validation split; results and discussion. PteroSet Zenodo v5, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21829388: record API manifest compared with the local catalog; 4,096-byte HTTP 206 range of metadata_v2.csv used to inspect only its header; row values were not reviewed or saved. microsoft/PteroSet commit b6aaf57ac32f93715e3570538f3580a78a80b741: targeted raw source files fetched transiently for static review; no code executed. Checked 2026-10-13.
study_snapshot: The v5 record describes 563 time-lapse recordings (73.62 hours), 15,372 broad bird-event annotations, 6,702 species-level determinations and 168 species. Data were collected with AudioMoth recorders in Colombia between 2023 and 2025.

Each time-lapse file concatenates a 10-second sample from each 30-minute interval. PteroSet v5 adds a segment_manifest.csv to map those segments. A timestamp in the concatenated file is not evidence of continuous intervening behavior or an animal reply.

Four experienced annotators used acoustic and spectrogram review and retained clearly identifiable signals. Strong labels mark time and frequency bounds; the binary baseline marks a five-second window positive when any bird annotation overlaps it. No independent behavior or receiver-response labels are included.

The paper uses five leave-one-project-out folds and non-overlapping evaluation windows. Four projects are different seasons at Puerto Asís; MAP1 is at Pivijay. Thus only one fold holds out a distinct named landscape, while the other four share the broad Puerto Asís landscape between train and test.

The exact Zenodo v5 record declares CC BY 4.0 and lists 12 files (86.4 GB), including annotations and a checkpoint archive. Its 12 provider-reported names, sizes and MD5 strings match the catalog, but no dataset bytes were hashed. A transient 4,096-byte HTTP 206 range of metadata_v2.csv was used to inspect only the header, which exposes location_id, recorder_id, date_recorded, latitude and longitude; row values were not reviewed or saved. The linked code repository declares MIT. The pinned reader names Zenodo record 21829388, while the downloader follows the concept DOI's latest version by default; the README example also names metadata.csv. The reader contains a debugger breakpoint and emits precise coordinates. Checkpoint lineage and upstream initialization terms remain unresolved. No dataset files or code were saved or executed.

Keep PteroSet as a detection-method comparator, not the first context/communication benchmark. Consider a reproducibility review only if an independent specialist agrees the detection question is useful and location handling is acceptable; then resolve the moving-version downloader, debugger and stale example, define a frozen grouped split, and inspect only the minimum joins needed under a documented privacy plan.

No dataset rows or species-specific locations were retrieved, reviewed or published; the markers do not imply that every recording is at the town center.

title: OpenSoundscape: bioacoustic tools, not animal translation
seo_description: OpenSoundscape supports audio analysis, Raven annotations, detection and localization. These tools can organize evidence, but they do not decode animal meaning.
kind: Research software and strongly labeled bird-soundscape dataset
year_label: Software paper (2023); current code release reviewed separately
review_stage: Selected paper sections, versioned repository/license, annotation tutorial, dataset record and Dryad policy reviewed; no code or data executed
review_depth: Reviewed the paper abstract, software overview, annotation and localization functionality, examples, and stated scope; the official v0.13.2 release and tagged MIT license; the official annotation tutorial; and the Dryad dataset landing page and repository-wide license policy. The article describes v0.9.1, the repository lists v0.13.2 as its latest release, while the stable annotation tutorial still pins 0.13.1. No package, code, model, recording, archive, or annotation row was downloaded, installed, or run. The publisher marks the article Open Access, but its exact reuse license was not visible in the reviewed page. No independent software or biological review occurred.
finding: OpenSoundscape is a Python research toolkit for manipulating audio and spectrograms, working with Raven time-frequency annotations, preparing labels, training or applying acoustic classifiers, detecting periodic calls, and localizing sounds from synchronized recorders. Its 2023 paper describes version 0.9.1; the current official release page lists v0.13.2. This is useful infrastructure for acoustic observation and researcher workflows, not a model that translates animal communication. The linked Dryad dataset is a distinct resource: its current landing page reports 385 minutes of bird soundscape recordings across four days, 48 species and 16,052 strong annotations. These labels support bounded detection or classification tasks; they do not establish call meaning or receiver understanding.
limitations: The tool is a Python analysis package, not a beginner mobile app, persistent recording service, or general animal-language system. The tutorial's pinned package version trails the newest release, so any reproduction must pin and verify the version actually used. The tagged MIT code license does not license dependencies, model-zoo code, checkpoints, tutorial media, or datasets. Dryad's current policy says repository data are CC0, but the reviewed item page did not expose an item-level license field; reconfirm the exact version terms before reuse. The dataset's four recording days and one named reserve do not demonstrate broad geographic or individual-level generalization. No files, labels, or data splits were independently inspected.
lesson: Keep the Field Companion simple and human-led. If researchers identify a real need, an advanced export/review path could exchange human-marked acoustic intervals with established annotation tools while preserving observers' notes separately from model predictions. Do not add OpenSoundscape or its models to the mobile app merely because the package is open source; first validate a synthetic, version-pinned workflow and review every dependency and data component.
next_review: Only after an independent researcher identifies a concrete workflow gap, test a small synthetic Talk2Nature WAV and human annotation through the exact OpenSoundscape release and a documented Raven-compatible export/import path. Record dependency versions and data-rights boundaries. Do not acquire the 1.18 GB Dryad package or train a model until a bounded task, exact file terms, leakage-safe split and qualified review are in place. AutoResearch remains NOT READY.
expert_review: No independent bioacoustic, research-software, or animal-communication specialist has reviewed this assessment.
review_locator: Lapp et al. (2023): abstract, software overview, Raven integration, examples, and scope; official repository v0.13.2 README/LICENSE; stable audio-annotation tutorial; Chronister et al. Dryad record and Dryad mission page.
study_snapshot: Python toolkit for audio/spectrogram handling, annotations, acoustic detection/classification and synchronized-recorder localization.
The tutorial represents human labels as time-frequency boxes and shows Raven import/export and label preparation; an annotated event is not automatically a communicative meaning.
The paper describes v0.9.1; the official repository lists v0.13.2; the stable annotation tutorial currently installs v0.13.1. Pin the tested version.
Dryad version updated 2021-04-06 lists 4 files totaling 1.18 GB; the landing page reports 385 minutes across four days, 48 species and 16,052 annotations.
Keep paper, software and dataset as separate metadata-only components. No code, model, recording or dataset bytes were acquired or run.

atlas.location_note: This note reviews software and a dataset landing page, not verified participant or field-observation coordinates.

title: HyenaSET: a strong sound-event benchmark, not a communication test
seo_description: HyenaSET offers 243 hours of expert-reviewed hyena vocalizations and an individual-held-out split. Its rights and baseline limit reuse.
year_label: bioRxiv v2 preprint; Edmond dataset v1
review_stage: Targeted preprint methods and results; official dataset version, file and terms metadata
review_depth: Read the bioRxiv v2 abstract and targeted data-collection, annotation, split, benchmark and data/code-availability sections. Examined official Edmond and DataCite metadata for version 1, release date, archive size, provider checksum and dataset terms. The paper is a preprint, not peer-reviewed. No audio, labels, code or model weights were downloaded, installed or run; no data rows, coordinates or individual timestamps were inspected. No independent review or reproduction occurred.
finding: HyenaSET is a useful recent sound-event methods comparator: its Edmond v1 metadata describes 590,480 ten-second clips, about 1,640 hours from 19 spotted hyenas, with 87,394 expert-reviewed clips (about 243 hours). The annotations mark vocalization intervals and types, and distinguish calls from the collar-wearing focal hyena from nearby non-focal callers. The preprint provides sample-stratified splits and a four-individual held-out split, then reports an animal2vec baseline. These targets concern event detection, call categories and source attribution; they are not independently observed receiver responses or evidence of message meaning.
limitations: The bioRxiv manuscript is not peer-reviewed. Edmond's v1 archive is one 107,184,528,475-byte TAR.GZ with a provider MD5 that Talk2Nature has not locally verified. Its dataset-specific terms are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so the data are not admitted to the shared commercial-capable training path; the preprint, animal2vec code and model weights have separate rights. The record describes a CSV that maps randomized names to individual identities and recording times for four test individuals; no rows or precise locations were reviewed, so wildlife-location sensitivity remains unresolved. The preprint says animal2vec is pretrained on all available audio before fine-tuning on the first cross-validation split. That wording implies exposure to audio from held-out partitions; our methods interpretation is that the reported result is transductive unless the authors clarify otherwise, not a strict unseen-audio baseline. No independently observed behavior or receiver-response labels were established by this review.
lesson: A useful design reference can still be unusable as project training data. Preserve event boundaries, focal/non-focal attribution, quiet intervals, animal-held-out tests and a separate record of what data a representation model sees during pretraining. A held-out label split is not a clean generalization test if unlabeled test audio entered pretraining. Keep signal detection and source attribution separate from independently observed context, receiver response and meaning.
next_review: Keep the records metadata-only. Before considering a separate non-commercial reproduction, have a qualified bioacoustics and machine-learning reviewer inspect the exact label dictionary, group manifests, pretraining exposure and wildlife metadata; first establish a concrete question that this 107 GB collar-recorded dataset can answer. Do not acquire it or use its weights in the shared project path without a scoped rights, privacy and evaluation review.
expert_review: No independent bioacoustics or machine-learning specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature assessment.

The dataset description lists five sample-stratified splits and a four-individual held-out split. The preprint says the animal2vec baseline is pretrained on all available audio before fine-tuning on the first split.
Dataset: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Preprint: CC BY 4.0. Code and weights are separate. The preprint reports a micro-average AP of 0.86; Talk2Nature did not reproduce it.

title: CowRumIA: a cattle-audio app and a test-set caution
seo_description: CowRumIA pairs cattle vocalization labels with a Flutter Android app. A pinned review explains why its reported 85.6% score is not an untouched test result.
kind: Mobile app, dataset and machine-learning methods review
year_label: GitHub repository snapshot at pinned commit; Zenodo dataset v1.0.0
review_stage: Pinned GitHub README, LICENSE and training-script static review; official Zenodo v1 metadata review
review_depth: Read the pinned CowRumIA README and LICENSE, statically inspected model/train_model.py around its split, callbacks and final evaluation, and reviewed the Zenodo v1 record description, file listing, dates and Rights section. The repository snapshot was pinned to commit 44fdc5e5cf3f080457211bb87eb8cb2fc6b099ac. No dataset or model files were downloaded, no code was run, no app was built, no thesis full text was reviewed, and no independent specialist review or reproduction occurred.
finding: CowRumIA is a 2026 undergraduate project pairing a Flutter Android app with YAMNet embeddings and a dense classifier for four cattle vocalization categories. The Zenodo v1 record describes 624 labeled WAVs; the README reports 194 stressed beef, 39 calm beef, 350 stressed dairy and 41 calm dairy samples and advertises 85.6% accuracy on 125 test audios. In the pinned training script, a random stratified 80/20 utterance split creates X_test, then the same X_test and y_test are supplied to training as validation data while callbacks select epochs and adjust the learning rate; predictions are later evaluated on that same set. The reported score therefore is not an untouched final-test estimate. The size or direction of any resulting optimism cannot be determined from this review. This is a useful mobile-implementation comparator and a strong evaluation-design lesson, not evidence of animal communication or a validated welfare diagnostic.
limitations: The four output classes jointly encode cattle production type and stress/calm category, and the README class counts are imbalanced (350 in the largest class versus 39 in the smallest). The split code is utterance-level and does not group by animal, session or site; the reviewed materials do not establish whether repeated animals or recording conditions cross splits. Zenodo states expert validation but the reviewed record does not provide the annotation protocol, inter-rater agreement or independent operational welfare ground truth. The dataset contains mixed-source material, but upstream, file-level reuse terms are unresolved; Zenodo shows only a copyright notice. GitHub declares MIT for repository software, while the packaged TFLite assets and underlying YAMNet/model-weight provenance and terms were not separately verified. The README describes an intensity-weighted stress-level output and a confidence threshold, but the relationship to independently measured welfare severity is not established here. Its documented training command points to a file that returned 404 at the pinned commit. No effect size, clinical/welfare utility, device reliability, field performance or cross-site generalization was reproduced. These are limits of the reviewed evidence, not proof that the project authors have no additional records.
lesson: For mobile animal-audio tools, keep capture and review flows distinct from a diagnostic claim. Reserve validation data for model selection and protect a separate locked test set; group splits by the biological and recording units that could carry shared signal. Evaluate class-specific errors, calibration and simple context/background baselines, and define behavior labels with qualified domain reviewers. A phone interface and an accuracy number do not establish welfare value, message meaning or transfer to another species.
next_review: Keep the Zenodo audio and all model assets metadata-only. Before considering any dataset or model use, resolve dataset and upstream file-level rights, inspect the annotation protocol and available animal/session/site grouping fields, and obtain cattle-welfare and bioacoustics review. For a separately justified benchmark, define an independently observed target, compare majority/context/background/acoustic baselines, select group-held-out validation and a locked test, and report macro-F1, per-class recall, calibration and clustered uncertainty. Resolve the missing documented training path before claiming an exact reproduction. No Talk2Nature training or welfare-facing output is recommended from the materials reviewed.
expert_review: No independent cattle-welfare, bioacoustics or machine-learning specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature assessment.

title: Playback can shape the call you measure
seo_description: A five-budgerigar experiment found playback context changed conditioned call intensity and variation; it did not test call meaning or a consumer app.
review_depth: PubMed citation/abstract and selected PMC author-manuscript sections surfaced by the article index—subjects, apparatus, stimuli, procedures, analyses, and results/discussion—reviewed 2026-10-14. The listed supplement, raw data, and code were not inspected; no reanalysis, replication, or independent review. Reuse terms were not verified.
finding: Five individually housed budgerigars had been trained to call after a visual LED cue, with food reinforcement. In a call-plus-flock condition, calls were louder than in silent, call-only, flock-only, and pure-tone conditions. Among the three birds that produced non-primary calls, these calls were more likely in the call-plus-flock and call-only conditions than in silent, flock-only, and tone conditions. The result shows acoustic context can modulate a trained vocal response in this laboratory setup; it does not decode a message.
limitations: The study involved five birds (one male, four females), not a household population or a held-out-individual test. The animals were trained in an operant setup and the experimental conditions followed a fixed sequence; this was not passive observation of spontaneous calls. The call-variation result applied to three birds. Vocal intensity and call form are not measures of comprehension, welfare benefit, or semantic meaning, and no receiver-response test was reported. The paper describes maintaining birds at 85–90% of free-feeding weight during the experiment and reports institutional animal-care approval; this protocol should not be copied as consumer-app guidance. The PMC record lists supplementary material, but it was not inspected. Raw data/code and their rights were not established in this review.
lesson: Playback is an intervention: it can change the vocal output being measured, even when the emitted call is already trained. Keep Talk2Nature's public observation tools passive and silent. Any future playback or receiver experiment needs its own specialist-led welfare and protocol review; this result is not evidence that an app can talk to or translate a parrot.
next_review: Inspect the supplement and complete analysis details, verify applicable article reuse terms, and obtain independent avian-behavior and statistical review before using this as more than a bounded methods comparator. Keep playback out of the public app.
expert_review: Not independently reviewed by an avian-behavior or statistical specialist.
review_stage: Selected methods and results reviewed

Silence, conspecific call plus flock sound, call only, flock sound only, and a pure tone.
Call-plus-flock trials had louder calls; three birds also showed more non-primary calls in call-rich conditions.
The article reports institutional animal-care approval and a restricted-weight protocol. It tested conditioned vocal output, not message meaning or receiver comprehension.

title: A camera can decode a known bee signal—with calibration
seo_description: A 2017 honeybee study decoded known waggle dances from calibrated infrared video, not arbitrary animal gestures or consumer-phone footage.
review_depth: Targeted PLOS ONE full-text sections reviewed: abstract, communication background, recording setup, target features, software modules, validation/results, discussion and license. The official GitHub README, API metadata and complete recursive tree were reviewed at pinned commit 3aaa5099aac698bd08df1d55f4cd5183d32f7e7d. Selected setup, validation, runtime and rights sections of the related 2015 Frontiers system paper were reviewed. No data, video, code, weights or supporting files were downloaded or executed; no reproduction or independent review.
finding: Wario et al. built a pipeline to detect honeybee waggle runs from a one-frame observation hive, estimate run orientation and duration, and map dances back to the field. The experiment used a small colony of 2,000 Apis mellifera carnica and one modified high-speed camera on each side of the comb, with infrared illumination. The paper specifies about 100 frames per second and at least 1.5 pixels per millimeter. Its temporal CNN filtered candidate image sequences; 8,239 manually labeled detections from two days were used, with 20% reserved for validation. The authors report 90.07% validation accuracy, corresponding to 89.8% recall at 95% precision. Orientation was compared with eight human tracers on 200 waggle runs, with mean error −2.92° and SD 7.37°. In a five-hour illustration, 571 detected dances from bees trained to a feeder 342 m southwest of the hive clustered around the feeder direction. This decodes a predefined, previously studied signal against a known physical outcome; the algorithm does not discover what arbitrary animal movements mean.
limitations: The 90.07% figure is validation performance, not an independent colony-, site-, camera- or season-held-out result in the reviewed account. The work concerns one species, a specialized observation hive, controlled illumination and a known feeder; translating waggle duration to distance required empirical calibration with known locations. The map aggregates dances and their run measurements; it is not a natural-language exchange with a bee. The author-linked repository is pinned to commit 3aaa5099aac698bd08df1d55f4cd5183d32f7e7d, but GitHub reports no recognized license and its inspected tree has no LICENSE/COPYING file, so the code, compiled module and ground-truth data remain metadata-only. A separate 2015 BeesBook system paper describes a more elaborate tracking setup; its image-analysis pipeline took about 500 times real time on one processor for that paper's long-term dataset, while its supercomputer run used about 1,000 processors. That figure is not a runtime measurement of the 2017 waggle-run detector, but it illustrates why camera claims must be tied to the exact task and hardware.
lesson: For Talk2Nature, start visual work with a signal whose features and external reference are already defined. A useful first camera workflow would preserve time, device/setup, human-reviewed event markers and uncertainty; model outputs must remain separate from observations. Ordinary-phone suitability is an open measurement question. Do not describe the Field Companion as a general gesture translator or add animal-directed playback based on this result.
next_review: Ask independent insect-behavior and computer-vision reviewers whether the validation and manual-angle comparison support the bounded detection/orientation claims, which colony/day/camera holdout would test transfer, and what minimum capture setup is needed. Before any app camera pilot, define a passive question, privacy/retention and consent rules, animal-welfare review, a known external criterion and a device feasibility test. Keep linked code and data metadata-only until component terms and provenance are resolved.
expert_review: No independent insect-behavior or computer-vision specialist has reviewed this Talk2Nature assessment.

Detect candidate waggle runs and estimate their duration and orientation; a separate mapping stage uses known solar azimuth and feeder-distance calibration.
The CNN used 8,239 manually labeled detections from two days; 20% was reserved for validation. Reported accuracy was 90.07%, or 89.8% recall at 95% precision.
Eight coworkers supplied reference angles for 200 waggle runs. In a five-hour demonstration, 571 mapped dances clustered around a known feeder 342 m southwest.
The article is CC BY 4.0. The pinned GitHub code/data repository has no recognized license or LICENSE/COPYING file in the inspected tree; no files were acquired.

title: Barkopedia: context labels do not show call meaning
seo_description: Barkopedia's dog activity and environment task predicts video-assisted labels from audio; source-media rights, annotation and split details remain unresolved.
review_stage: Official challenge and one task-specific dataset card reviewed; Task 6 card history checked only; metadata-only
review_depth: Reviewed the official Barkopedia README and MIT LICENSE at GitHub commit ef8da9155e101cb76d4ee260bebb4d4fde4c2a1d; opened the linked task Spaces; reviewed the Activity and Environment dataset card and Hugging Face revision/tree at 60a721a7f9477634971f6b3df29dc2a5e56994d8. The README says source audio was collected from YouTube and Reddit and lists eight tasks. Only the Activity and Environment task card was examined; no academic challenge-results paper or final leaderboard report was reviewed. No archive, CSV, audio, code or model was downloaded or executed, and no independent reproduction or specialist review occurred. On October 14, also inspected the exact Hugging Face Task 6 card revision and its README diff: the former Barkopedia emotion card was rewritten as EmotionalCanines and changed its license metadata, but this does not establish dataset-file continuity. No Task 6 audio, labels or archives were inspected; the Activity and Environment card remains the only Barkopedia task-specific dataset card reviewed.
finding: Barkopedia was an IJCAI 2025 challenge with eight dog-audio tasks: age, sex, breed, individual recognition, activity/environment, emotion, vocal separation and vocal detection. Its README describes the corpus as real-world clips sourced from YouTube and Reddit. The reviewed Activity and Environment card lists 12,480 training clips and 3,120 test clips, with eight activity categories and six environment categories. It says labels were initially generated through video-assisted inference with Janus-Pro-7B and later manually verified. This is a useful context-label classification comparator, but it does not show that an audio prediction represents an animal's intended message, subjective state or a validated welfare outcome. The pinned Hugging Face tree includes train, validation and test directories, although the card still says the test set will be released later. Its Dataset Viewer reports incompatible audiofolder/CSV formats across splits. The Barkopedia GitHub repository is the MIT-licensed challenge site/documentation; its inspected root tree did not include a training or evaluation implementation.
limitations: The challenge timeline ended in 2025. No final leaderboard, peer-reviewed benchmark report, baseline implementation or seven other task-specific dataset cards were reviewed. The card does not specify per-recording source permissions, consent/privacy, annotator qualifications, blinded review, inter-annotator agreement, animal/session/site grouping or an untouched locked-test protocol. Its MIT metadata and the GitHub site's MIT LICENSE do not independently establish rights to source-platform recordings. The Viewer format error and card's future-tense test-set text show that the public metadata is not fully synchronized, but do not prove the audio files are unusable. No data, labels or sound were inspected, so no model performance or dataset quality conclusion is claimed. The former Barkopedia Task 6 Hugging Face card was later rewritten to describe EmotionalCanines and now links a separate dataset repository. Its README history does not establish that the historical challenge files and the EmotionalCanines release are the same data; do not treat the current card as a verified Task 6 dataset review.
lesson: Keep three claims separate: an audio classifier can predict a dataset's context labels; labels may be derived with video and human review; neither alone demonstrates call meaning or independently observed behavior. For Talk2Nature, retain observer-entered behavior and model predictions as separate records. Do not use this dataset in a model run until the exact recordings' rights, annotation process, grouping and evaluation splits are resolved.
next_review: If this benchmark becomes a candidate, first verify the exact source-media terms and consent basis, the complete annotation workflow and agreement, and individual/session/site membership in train, validation and test. Pin a reproducible baseline and compare against context-only and simple acoustic controls before any model run. If these records are unavailable, retain this as a metadata-only comparator and use a separately rights-cleared, independently labeled question for Talk2Nature.

title: Amazon parrot dialects across 22 years: cultural change, not call meaning
seo_description: A 22-year yellow-naped Amazon call study reports shifting dialects. Its Dryad data contains measurements, not raw audio or receiver-response tests.
kind: Longitudinal contact-call dialect study and data review
review_stage: Abstract-level paper review plus Dryad dataset/API and pinned-code metadata review
review_depth: Reviewed the article abstract and targeted Methods/Results passages surfaced through the PMC search index; direct publisher retrieval returned HTTP 403 and the PMC page presented a bot check, so the full article and supplements were not reviewed. Reviewed the Dryad v6 landing-page data dictionary and rights statement, current Dryad reuse guide, TLS-verified API version/file manifest, and the GitHub README, license metadata, pinned tree and setup/input sections of four R Markdown analyses. No dataset bytes were acquired; no code or model was executed.
finding: The paper's abstract reports that learned yellow-naped Amazon contact-call dialects shifted between 2005 and 2016: more sites used multiple call types, formerly distinct northern and southern regions became more acoustically similar, and new variants and greater acoustic variation appeared. The authors place these observations alongside a period of population decline. The version-6 Dryad deposit documents measurements and metadata for surveys in 1994, 2005 and 2016, but not the underlying audio.
limitations: The reported temporal association does not show that population decline caused the vocal changes, nor that dialect changes altered receiver behavior, fitness or call meaning. This review is not full text: detailed statistical methods and supplements were not inspected. Dryad v6 lists 2,461 selected calls, 2,461 acoustic-measurement rows and 56 site-year rows; the selection table uses human visual/aural call-type labels, and BirdID is unique only within a site-year, not a stable cross-year identity. Raw audio and roost-count data are not in the deposit. The author README says exact site coordinates are withheld, while site names appear in the metadata; the atlas therefore uses only the existing country-scale Costa Rica locator. The code is MIT-licensed but its current reproducibility is limited by author-specific paths, unpinned dependencies and absent input files. File download failed with HTTP 401/403 in this environment; no bytes were acquired.
lesson: This is a useful longitudinal example of vocal culture and dialect structure, not evidence of translation. Preserve call type, recording year, site-year, within-site-year caller ID, acoustic quality/overlap and provenance as distinct fields. Do not randomly split individual calls and claim unseen-site, unseen-year or meaning generalization. A future receiver-response question would need separate behavioral labels and experimental evidence.
next_review: If the official Dryad download becomes accessible through the documented public route, first verify the three small tabular files against the v6 SHA-256 manifest and run only a local structure/grouping audit. Before any baseline, obtain full-text/supplement review and qualified independent parrot-bioacoustics and statistical review; keep raw audio, exact sites and training admission out of scope.

title: EmotionalCanines: video-derived labels are not a dog-reported emotion
seo_description: EmotionalCanines predicts video-derived dog arousal and valence labels from bark audio; it does not show call meaning or a validated emotion readout.
taxon: Domestic dog (Canis familiaris), Siberian Husky and Shiba Inu
review_stage: Targeted full-text methods/results review; version-pinned dataset metadata review; no independent reproduction
review_depth: Read the author-hosted eight-page ACM Multimedia paper sections on dataset generation, annotation, reliability, dog-separated splits, baselines, results and limitations. Reviewed the exact Hugging Face card commit c0617b15562882b9eee4cc1bcb8e6aa80e51bd34 and its README diff, plus the pinned GitHub README/LICENSE at 6b73c5fce55fc132e97db6a76899f8594a955f59. The paper reports 1,400 bark sequences (700 per breed; 600 train and 100 test per breed) from 199 dogs, with dog identities separated between train and test. Twelve annotators contributed; each sequence received three labels, and a 100-sample pilot reported Fleiss kappa 0.30 for arousal and 0.42 for valence. No recordings, labels, code or model weights were downloaded or run; no metrics were reproduced.
finding: The paper predicts two three-class labels from audio: arousal (low/medium/high) and valence (negative/neutral/positive). Annotators first watched the associated video with surrounding context and used visible behavior and situation to assign the labels; samples were retained only when at least two of three raters agreed on both dimensions. These are human video-derived behavior/affect annotations, not an animal-reported state, an independently validated physiological measure, a receiver response, or evidence that a bark means a particular thing. The article reports dog-separated tests with best accuracies around 50–57% across breed and target combinations. It separately reports higher 10-fold cross-validation results, but the reviewed methods do not specify whether those folds were grouped by dog. The Hugging Face path formerly used for Barkopedia Task 6 was rewritten at the pinned revision as EmotionalCanines and its license metadata changed; no continuity of the underlying files was verified.
limitations: The paper says its source pipeline began from internet video-derived bark sequences and acknowledges engagement-related sampling bias. The emotion labels depend on human interpretation of video behavior/context; the 100-sample pilot reports fair agreement, not external ground truth, and the authors discuss the difficulty of directly measuring subjective state from visible behavior. The dataset covers two breeds and only 35 minutes of bark sequences; each breed has 100 held-out test sequences. The reported 10-fold CV grouping is not clear from the reviewed methods, and no baseline code or results were independently reproduced. The dataset repositories declare CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, but permissions, consent and privacy terms for original source videos were not independently traced. Do not treat audio classification as emotion diagnosis, welfare advice or communication translation.
lesson: For Talk2Nature, store a person’s directly observed behavior separately from model output and from any inferred affect. If an affect question is ever studied, predefine the behavioral/physiological evidence and independent validation; avoid presenting a video-derived human label as the animal’s inner state.
next_review: Before considering any dataset use, resolve the original video/audio permissions, consent and privacy basis, identify whether the current GitHub and historical Hugging Face files are the same release, and obtain specialist review of the annotation construct. title: El Silencio helps detect sound across taxa, not decode meaning

review_stage: Full overview paper, pinned annotation protocol and dataset/benchmark-fit review
review_depth: Queried official Zenodo API metadata for labeled record 17064353 and unlabeled record 17122738, including publication dates, record-level licenses, file counts, byte totals and provider MD5 values. finding: El Silencio is a useful multi-taxon sound-event detection candidate: the paper describes 770 one-minute soundscapes (12.8 hours) and about 15,000 event boxes across birds, mammals, amphibians and insects. The manual protocol labels acoustic group, call/sonotype and sound form; it groups same-species signals separated by no more than one second. These acoustic/taxonomic labels do not supply independently observed behavior, caller intent or receiver-response labels. The paper's BirdCLEF+ competition dataset is a separate sound-identification task, so its classification score is not a result on this El Silencio subset and does not measure communication. This can help test a multi-species detection/data workflow, but it is not a communication or meaning benchmark.
limitations: The paper's unlabeled snapshot is 11,340 recordings at 63 sites; the later pinned README and separate Zenodo deposit describe 10,980 recordings at 61 sites (360 fewer across two sites), with no explanation in reviewed sources. The protocol's explicit group codes are birds, anurans and insects, while the paper describes four taxa including mammals; the mapping needs specialist clarification. No inter-annotator reliability statistic was reported in the reviewed paper/protocol. The labeled Zenodo page displays 109.8 GB while its nine-file API inventory totals 3,546,609,904 bytes; unresolved. The unlabeled API inventory lists 61 ZIPs totaling 49,620,235,222 bytes. Zenodo declares CC BY 4.0 at record level; source-media rights, consent/privacy, human-audio handling and sensitive-location conditions remain unreviewed. UNKNOWN is not a stable class. No audio, annotations or split were inspected, and no baseline was run. Event detection, acoustic association and communication meaning remain different claims.
lesson: Use multi-taxonomic soundscapes to check whether the tool can locate and organize candidate events across animal groups. Keep a human-reviewed event label separate from behavior observed in context, model predictions and any claim about meaning. A pretrained encoder may organize acoustic patterns; grounded communication claims still require independent behavioral observations and receiver-side tests.
next_review: Ask a qualified bioacoustics reviewer to resolve the protocol's taxonomic-label scope, annotation consistency and appropriate use. Seek provider clarification for the 11,340/63 versus 10,980/61 release change and the labeled record page/API size discrepancy; review source-media rights, privacy, human-audio and location safeguards before acquiring any sample. If a concrete detector question remains, pre-register a small rights-cleared evaluation with site-held-out splits and a simple baseline before running a model. This dataset does not satisfy the first context/meaning benchmark gates.

title: CEB can benchmark bird sound detection, not what a call means

review_stage: Official Zenodo v1.1 record, version notes, schema and API file inventory reviewed; annotation rows, media and model remain uninspected

finding: CEB v1.1 is a large library of bird recordings with human-marked sound events: 20,826 audio files and 92,857 annotations across 256 eBird species codes and 21 vocalization types. It can help test whether software finds and sorts labeled calls in recordings. It contains no independent observations of a listener's response or ground truth about what a bird meant, so it cannot test translation. The field soundscape recordings are more relevant to passive-monitoring workflows than the separate focal Xeno-Canto recordings.
limitations: The full collection is 49.7 GB. train_soundscape uses weak point-centered labels with a fixed +/-2.5 second window; many rows have no vocalization type. The smaller 2,401,049-byte test_soundscape.csv contains public test labels and was not inspected; it is not a concealed locked test, and a separate untouched evaluation would be needed. The data are mostly from Germany with a smaller Greek subset and are not a parrot-specific context corpus. The record gives CC BY 4.0 for soundscape audio and all dataset metadata/annotations, while train_xenocanto retains per-record Xeno-Canto licenses; the schema says some of those license fields are empty. The schema also identifies 40 zero-area boxes that must be excluded from localization tasks and one truncated Xeno-Canto audio file whose annotations extend beyond its duration. No project/site leakage, source overlap, annotation reliability or source-media privacy audit has been performed.
lesson: Use a large bird collection to test whether software can find and organize labeled sounds. Keep these acoustic categories separate from independently observed behavior, a receiver's response and any claim of meaning. The best species for a later communication-focused study may still be a companion parrot, but CEB does not answer that question.
next_review: CEB remains a separate detection-engineering candidate, not the first communication-adjacent ML question. If the training-table group audit is still worth pursuing, first prepare a bounded, rights- and privacy-reviewed intake plan that fits an explicitly reviewed integrity limit; do not inspect the public test-label CSV as a locked evaluation. title: BirdSet: a large bird-sound benchmark, not animal translation
seo_description: BirdSet is a large bird-sound classification benchmark. It tests acoustic recognition, not animal meaning or conversation.
review_stage: Targeted primary paper, live dataset-card and maintainer license-thread review; no data acquisition or reproduction
review_depth: Reviewed the primary arXiv abstract and version history, the current BirdSet dataset card and its configuration/metadata/license descriptions, and the complete maintainer clarification thread on mixed per-record licenses. No paper body, audio, labels, code or weights were acquired or run; no independent specialist reviewed this note.
review_locator: arXiv:2403.10380v6 abstract and version history; BirdSet card: dataset configuration table, metadata and licensing sections; DBD-research-group/BirdSet issue 337, May 2026 maintainer/contributor discussion.
finding: BirdSet is a large benchmark for recognizing bird species and related acoustic labels in recordings and soundscapes. The paper reports more than 6,800 recording hours, nearly 10,000 training classes and eight strongly labeled evaluation datasets totaling more than 400 hours. The live card lists a 528,434-recording XCL snapshot at 484 GB and recommends a regional HSN configuration with 5,460 training recordings, 10,296 test labels and 21 classes at 5.92 GB. These are upstream-reported benchmark figures, not a Talk2Nature reproduction. The task is acoustic classification; it does not test whether a receiver understood a call or what it meant.
limitations: BirdSet is not parrot-specific and does not contain the receiver-response or validated behavior labels needed for a communication claim. Its card declares CC BY-NC 4.0 at the collection level and limits the dataset to non-commercial research and education, while individual Xeno-Canto recordings carry mixed terms; the maintainer thread records corrected metadata and a mix that includes CC BY, CC0, SA and NC-SA entries. The interaction between collection-level limits and individual rights remains unresolved, so no subset is admitted for Talk2Nature training or commercial use. The card itself is not revision-pinned, its compatibility notes conflict, and the live dataset viewer cannot load its custom script. Location fields are present and would need careful treatment.
lesson: A big dataset can help build and measure a perception layer—such as detecting a species or acoustic event—but that output is not a translation. Keep sound detection, caller identity, observed context and receiver-supported meaning as separate research targets. For this project, BirdSet is a valuable methods reference; the separately gated fruit-bat context study and newly reviewed OpenWhistle dolphin benchmark are promising but distinct data-led candidates, while companion parrots remain a different community-observation and app-participation path.
next_review: Do not download or train on BirdSet now. If a future project needs a bird-classification baseline, first define whether the use is strictly non-commercial, pin the exact configuration and revision, get a component-level rights review, check any location fields, and compare it with a rights-cleared benchmark suited to the intended species. Keep biological communication claims dependent on independently observed context and receiver-response evidence.

finding: WABAD is a promising large-scale bird-acoustic reference. The publisher reports 5,047 minutes of audio with 91,931 species-level annotated vocalizations from 1,192 species, 72 recording sites, 29 locations and 13 biomes. The latest Zenodo record lists 21.3 GB. This scale could help researchers test whether a sound model detects and identifies bird vocalizations across sites. The reviewed task description concerns vocalization occurrence and species labels; it does not test a receiver's response or what a call means.

The archive's version history and publisher data statement point to different versions; the reuse discrepancy is unresolved. Source-recording provenance and per-file conditions were not audited. WABAD therefore remains a metadata-only research candidate, not an admitted training set or a Talk2Nature benchmark.
lesson: A large, multi-site bird dataset can teach us how well software finds and sorts vocalizations, and whether that skill travels across places. It cannot by itself teach us what a bird is communicating. Keep detected sound, human-observed context, an animal's measured response and any model prediction in separate records. Start with a small, rights-cleared detection question before attempting a meaning or conversation claim.

review_locator: arXiv:2609.34839v1, Sections 3–5 and 9–10; OpenWhistle-Pretraining revision eea37423c7841b0f99a7c0380f945999c0a2c489; OpenWhistle-Classification-Finetuning revision 2b7806e3c5913c459c40b824ab7f944d494b3993; OpenWhistle-Wav2Vec2.0 revision 985ac11bc6939af5e41383143aad5a0ae6993f68; pinned official OpenWhistle README (source 411) and LICENSE-DATA (source 412) at commit ad715bb3cf24c36f85b3c3c8159077548134a39e.
finding: OpenWhistle is a timely single-species research candidate: its authors report about 114 hours of 96 kHz recordings collected over five years from five known dolphins at Dolphin Reef in Eilat, plus 8,354 expert-annotated whistles in 10 categories. The authors describe the site as a semi-natural marine area open to the Gulf of Aqaba and say human–dolphin interactions are dolphin-initiated and voluntary. The official Hugging Face cards list 31,780 unlabeled audio segments and a separate labeled set split into 5,848 training, 1,253 validation and 1,253 test examples. Published tasks detect whistle presence or classify whistle type. These are upstream descriptions, not a Talk2Nature reproduction.
limitations: All recordings come from one site and a pod of five; the paper says results need validation on independent groups. Its labels cover whistle categories, including individual signature-whistle types, not experimentally established message meanings or receiver understanding. The main evaluation holds out recording sessions, not whole animals, and the expert labels cover only a short part of the five-year span; the labels are highly imbalanced. The official repository README and LICENSE-DATA declare CC BY 4.0 for the dataset releases, while the pinned Hugging Face dataset-card fields are null; code terms were not visible in the repository root and the separate model card says its license is unspecified. No files are admitted or acquired.
lesson: This is a strong newly reviewed large-data candidate for a bounded communication-adjacent benchmark, not evidence of dolphin translation. A useful contribution would need to go beyond repeating the published whistle classifier—for example, a carefully reviewed test of temporal and individual generalization if the available metadata and rights support it. Keep this research track distinct from a companion-parrot app: app participation and model training have different evidence, consent and welfare requirements.
next_review: The dataset-level license declaration is now documented. Before any data acquisition or training, ask independent cetacean-bioacoustics and ML reviewers whether a within-pod whistle-structure reproduction would be useful and whether a temporal or individual-generalization extension is defensible. If they approve, freeze a bounded dataset-only run card and consider a project-authored simple acoustic baseline; do not reuse the unlicensed/unclear source code or model weights unless their terms are clarified. Do not infer meaning from detection or classification, and do not create playback features from this dataset.

title: Parrot social ties track call variation, not call meaning
seo_description: A 2025 monk-parakeet study links social networks with call variation, not meaning or receiver understanding.
review_stage: Targeted article, deposit-metadata and pinned-repository review; metadata only
review_depth: Reviewed the published article abstract and targeted methods, results, discussion, data-access, ethics and rights passages using the primary full-text record and institutional copy; checked the 2023 voiceprint paper for sample overlap; reviewed the Zenodo record and the GitHub README/tree at a pinned revision. On October 24, rechecked Methods section 2.1 and confirmed the Barcelona study region and field dates for the atlas. The archive, raw recordings, code and model outputs were not acquired or run.
review_locator: Smeele et al. (2025), abstract and targeted Methods, Results, Discussion, Data accessibility, Ethics and copyright passages; Smeele et al. (2023), Results and study-sample description; Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.13906800; GitHub commit 395a622b18f3f55fd4efdcb9a093cc214f6fdf67.
finding: This study combines social-network observations with monk-parakeet vocalizations. It reports networks for 337 birds, relatedness for 100, and 5,599 vocalizations from 229 individuals over two years. Call-diversity associations varied by year; close affiliates had more dissimilar calls. These are observational associations, not evidence that a specific call carries a known message.
limitations: The exact 5,599-call and 229-bird totals match the 2023 monk-parakeet voiceprint paper, so this is a new analysis of an overlapping cohort, not an independent acoustic replication. The study does not test receiver responses or experimentally established meanings. The authors discuss active differentiation as an interpretation; the reported associations alone do not establish that cause. The Zenodo archive was not inspected, and the GitHub README says some required inputs are not shared. Its documented nest/UTM location fields make location review necessary before any mapping. No coordinates are reproduced here.
lesson: This work shows why social relationships and sound should be recorded as separate, linked evidence. A useful next study could test whether carefully observed social context improves a bounded caller-identity or call-variation task, with whole-bird and whole-session holdouts. title: V33DA: a zebra-finch caller benchmark, not a translation model

finding: V33DA is a caller-attribution task: given an already-detected zebra-finch vocalization and the birds visible at that moment, identify the bird that produced it. The pinned card reports 33,625 verified events from 10 physically distinct birds across three experiments, with synchronized audio, video and pose; caller labels derive from on-body accelerometer vibration. In the experiment-held-out split, all 5,829 BP05 events from three callers (brown, purple, yellow) form the test set. That is a genuine unseen-bird group according to the card, but not a clean explanation of generalization because several cohort conditions shift together. This is an engineering benchmark candidate, not a communication-meaning result.
limitations: Caller identity is not behavior, addressee, receiver response, intent or meaning. The full release comes from one aviary and recording geometry and excludes overlapping calls; 10 physical birds, not 33,625 events, are the independent animals. The BP05 test also changes experiment, group, year/date and cage; treat its outcome only as a bundled shift test. The session-disjoint split retains the same birds. The pinned GitHub tree lacks the v33da/data package imported by scripts/train.py, including dataset, feature and split modules; the split-preparation script writes date-based session and held-out-experiment labels only. The README advertises leave-one-bird-out, but that path and the trainer cannot be independently reproduced from this snapshot. Three small text files have verified hashes, but the sample Parquet says 100 rows while split JSON reports full-release totals; no sample-specific split or Parquet join has been verified. BP05 metadata names brown, purple, yellow and red, while the card and caller-count table list three callers. Red has no event-count group; whether it is a visible non-caller candidate or stale metadata is unknown. Candidate-set cardinality and chance baseline are therefore unknown. No media or Parquet bytes were inspected. The separate V33DA++ companion adds overlap and padded context buckets but still uses the same ten birds and supplies no independently observed receiver behavior; see the companion note.
lesson: Use V33DA only if the question is caller attribution. A future baseline should compare candidate-count chance with a simple candidate-aware model, exclude accelerometer/oracle labels and stable identity shortcuts, and keep complete physical birds and shared sessions out of train/test groups. The BP05 experiment-held-out score is a bundled shift test. Do not call caller prediction translation. For overlap handling and longer context, see the separate V33DA++ review; its repeated bucket is not an independent cohort.
next_review: Before any run, require a pinned code snapshot containing the imported v33da.data modules and an independently auditable leave-one-bird-out split.
