finding: The latest Zenodo v2 record describes 1,302 ten-minute forest soundscapes—about 217 hours—from 104 sites in four northeastern U.S. parks, with approximately 183,000 vocalization annotations. The version-pinned site_metadata.csv has 104 unique sites; recording_metadata.csv independently has the same 104 site IDs. Its site counts are ACAD 31, HBEF 24, KAWW 24 and MABI 25. The landing-page opening summary says KAWW has 20 sites, so the headline total is supported while that park breakdown remains inconsistent. The v2 README says 88 bird species, matching the publisher abstract and earlier v1; however, species_metadata.csv has 96 rows marked IsBird=Yes, all with nonzero annotation counts totaling 182,633. The species-count discrepancy therefore remains unresolved. This is a promising field-acoustics resource for event detection, localization and species classification, not a communication dataset.
limitations: The annotations identify vocalization events and species, not individual callers, observed social behavior, receiver response or call meaning. The site total of 104 is corroborated by two metadata tables and the README, but the landing page lists KAWW as 20 while site_metadata.csv has 24. The v2 README/publisher abstract say 88 bird species while the species table marks 96 rows as birds; the annotation total for those rows is 182,633, and the discrepancy is unresolved. The current record says annotators may combine consecutive same-species calls when pauses are under two seconds, and faint or unidentifiable events may remain unlabeled. Sampling differs by subset: SIMR is tied to point-count surveys across sites, while ACAD and MABI use selected clear mornings during peak breeding season. These choices matter for event recall, class balance and site/time holdouts. The archive is concentrated in four parks in one region and does not establish performance on household parrots, phones or other taxa. Site coordinates are present in the metadata; no values were published or mapped. The dataset record declares CC BY 4.0, while the article text is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; neither statement is an independent audit of every component or source-media provenance.
lesson: A large, strongly annotated bird collection can help test whether software finds and classifies vocalizations across field recordings. It cannot show what a bird meant or whether another bird understood it. Keep this detection track separate from the Egyptian-fruit-bat context question, V33DA caller attribution and the provisional parrot observation workflow.
next_review: Ask the authors to clarify the README/species-table definition difference and the KAWW landing-page/site-table difference. The four metadata files remain local and are not admitted to training or biological inference. Keep the full release metadata-only until a bounded rights/privacy plan and independent review pass.

finding: The Wytham Great Tit Song Dataset is an unusually dense wild-population resource: its authors report 109,963 annotated songs and 1,161,033 acoustic notes from more than 400 individual birds, collected in Wytham Woods, Oxfordshire, from 2020 to 2023. The complete current OSF API root lists 23 files totaling 12,184,678,510 bytes: 14 data files (12,184,652,639 bytes) and nine documentation files (25,871 bytes). The 2025 paper already trained a ViT metric-learning model on this corpus, generated 384-dimensional embeddings for all 109,963 songs, and used them to analyze repertoire similarity and demographic drivers of song culture. It then used automated clustering plus manual song categorization; the reported 0.87 validation accuracy belongs to a separate ResNet50 validation procedure. The dataset supports valuable song-structure and population-methods work, but it has no independently observed interaction context, receiver response or label for what a song means.
limitations: This is one wild population and dawn-singing research system, so its labels do not establish transfer to other sites, species, household phones or general communication. Dataset documentation says bird identity associated with a breeding attempt can be uncertain or a proxy when the bird was not caught. The ordinary shared package is not the approximately 9 TB of original continuous soundscapes used in preparation. The authors’ nestbox metadata documentation specifies location coordinates in British National Grid and says the coordinates are also included in main.csv; the OSF manifest separately lists a Wytham perimeter shapefile. We inspected these documentation descriptions only, not coordinate values or file contents. Treat those fields as potentially sensitive wildlife-location information: keep public geography coarse and exclude precise coordinates from any future derivatives unless an appropriate wildlife-location review establishes a need and safe handling. The complete 2026-10-24 API tree has 23 entries; the earlier same-day 14-entry result was a partial traversal of data/ and omitted docs/. All 23 normalized paths and byte sizes match the historical snapshot. The 2026-10-23 local manifest stored a malformed 63-character SHA-256 for docs/metadata/main.md. On October 25, the current 6,426-byte file matched the OSF API SHA-256 and MD5; the cause of the malformed historical string is unknown. The file content was not reviewed, and no other provider hash was recomputed. Annotation values, grouping keys and dataset-level splits remain unaudited. The prior ViT embeddings were calculated across all songs from the same corpus, so treating them as a held-out-individual baseline for a new Talk2Nature benchmark would be an invalid shortcut; this is an evaluation-design inference from the published training scope. The 2025 paper already covers the obvious deep-embedding, individual-similarity and demographic song-culture tasks. No independent specialist assessed this note.
lesson: A large corpus can teach us to measure patterns in animal sound before we try to interpret them. This dataset is a candidate for note, sequence and repertoire questions, not a conversation model. Keep it separate from the Egyptian-fruit-bat context-prediction candidate and provisional household-parrot app cohort. Any future model result should use whole-individual and time-aware grouping, compare simple acoustic baselines, and state that it predicts acoustic structure rather than meaning.

title: Bat auditory cortex anticipates call patterns, not their meaning
review_stage: Primary article full text reviewed; data/code repository metadata only
review_depth: Reviewed the full main article through PMC, including its question, sample, acoustic and neural recording methods, category definitions, results, discussion, data/code availability and article license. Read the GIN DOI landing-page metadata only. The 5.8 GiB archive, repository file list, README, scripts, supplementary information and peer-review file were not inspected or acquired. No independent specialist reviewed this Talk2Nature assessment.
review_locator: Babl, Röhrig & Hechavarría, Communications Biology 9:699 (2026), DOI 10.1038/s42003-026-10319-4; PMC13197462, main text; GIN DOI 10.12751/g-node.44wmeq, public landing page.
seo_description: A 2026 bat neuroscience study reports auditory-cortex patterns before calls. It examines call class and sequence structure, not what calls mean to another bat.
finding: In ten awake Seba’s short-tailed bats, the authors report auditory-cortex firing patterns associated with whether the animal produced an echolocation pulse or a social communication call, and whether some calls occurred singly or in short sequences. Neural activity tracked the number of social-call syllables before vocal onset; the corresponding relationship for echolocation-pulse count appeared after onset. This is evidence about neural activity around the animal’s own vocal production, not a decoded message or receiver response.
limitations: The study used invasive, synchronized neural and ultrasonic recordings from a small captive cohort. Its acoustic classes differ in frequency as well as behavioral role, so those factors are not fully separated by the headline comparison. The reported SVM analysis uses randomized call-event-by-neuron activity instances; the reviewed methods do not establish performance on held-out bats or recording sessions. The paper does not test receiver comprehension or communicative meaning. No analysis was reproduced, and the 5.8 GiB GIN archive and analysis code were not inspected.
lesson: Keep self-produced call patterns, external acoustic events and receiver responses as separate evidence types. This study supports modeling timing and sequence structure as useful signals; it does not justify mapping a bat call to an English phrase. Its specialized neurophysiology is a comparative-science reference, not a capture design for ordinary phones.
next_review: Before considering any archive work, inspect the exact GIN manifest, file-level content and component terms, then define a bounded research question and storage plan. Ask an independent bat-neurobiology reviewer whether call class and spectral content are adequately separated and whether the instance-level decoding supports any across-animal inference. Do not acquire the large archive or execute deposited code without that need and review.

title: V33DA++ adds overlapping calls and context, not meaning

Linked GitHub README and source commit e988b985e38909b40b2705cdad994e3d9307181e were checked for the advertised split and training path.
finding: V33DA++ is a companion to the physically verified zebra-finch caller-attribution dataset. Its card describes 3,784 reviewer-verified overlapping-call rows, 33,625 single-vocalizer events with plus/minus two seconds of context, and 3,784 overlapping events with the same context. The overlap_padded bucket repeats the overlap events with padding, so the provider's 41,193-row total is not 41,193 unique events. The recordings and all ten birds are the same as V33DA. The card suggests source separation, vocal-activity detection, audio-visual synchronization and active-speaker detection; caller evidence is anchored by on-body accelerometers, which are an oracle label source rather than an admissible predictor.
limitations: This is a signal-processing and attribution resource, not a communication or interaction dataset: the reviewed card does not supply independently observed behavior, addressee, receiver response, intent or call meaning labels. It adds temporal context and overlapping events, not new animals or an independent cohort; results remain bounded to the same ten finches and controlled recording setup. The provider lists 167 GB for the release. The linked code repository's current main is still commit e988b985e38909b40b2705cdad994e3d9307181e; scripts/train.py imports v33da.data modules absent from that tree, while the split-preparation script writes session and held-out-experiment date assignments but no auditable leave-one-bird-out folds. The code path is not reproducible from the reviewed snapshot. The dataset card declares CC BY 4.0, while preprocessing tools and code are separately licensed; these declarations are not independent clearance.
lesson: V33DA++ makes a useful method candidate for testing vocal-activity detection, overlapping-call handling or audio-visual synchronization after an executable, reviewable pipeline and defensible grouped evaluation exist. It cannot establish animal-language translation or receiver understanding. Do not treat bucket row totals as independent calls or the repeated padded bucket as new evidence.

Before any acquisition or run, require an immutable code revision with the imported data package, exact V33DA++ evaluation splits, a non-oracle baseline, rights review for all components, and independent avian-bioacoustics and ML/statistical assessment. title: Zebra-finches exchange calls with an interactive audio model
seo_description: A 2026 zebra-finch preprint tests call timing and acoustic adaptation with AI-driven audio. It does not translate animal language.
year_label: bioRxiv preprint v3; not peer reviewed
review_stage: Primary preprint and two separate Zenodo release records reviewed; no archive acquisition or reproduction
review_depth: Reviewed the full bioRxiv v3 main text, including Results, Discussion, Methods 1.1–1.7, data-availability statement and posted license, plus official Zenodo landing-page/API metadata for records 23024019 and 23047646. A metadata-only refresh of the official bioRxiv v3 page on October 24 confirmed its current title and that the title and abstract were updated; the full text was not re-reviewed in this refresh. The code/model record lists one ZIP; the separate data record lists 11 files, including four raw example recordings and processed archives. No archive internals, supplemental analyses or media payloads were downloaded or inspected; no code, weights or data were run; no independent specialist reviewed this assessment.
review_locator: James et al., "Leveraging AI-powered interactive playbacks to decipher rules of communication in zebra finches," bioRxiv 2026.02.12.705387 v3, posted March 23, 2026, DOI 10.64898/2026.02.12.705387; Zenodo code/model record 23024019, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23024019; separate Zenodo data record 23047646, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23047646.
finding: Female zebra-finches changed the timing and acoustic structure of their calls during exchanges. The paper reports more than 1,000 hours of recordings and analyzes 834,309 calls from 21 birds across 40 pair interactions in Methods; one Results passage says 20 birds, so the count is inconsistent. The authors define a response as a first call within one second after a partner's call ends. They report responses after about 44% of partner calls, compared with an estimated 10% chance level, and describe birds responding to live sounds from an interactive audio model in a controlled lab study. The model predicts patterns such as which bird may call next and when; this is evidence about acoustic timing and contingency, not a translation of calls into human language.
limitations: This is a preprint, not peer-reviewed evidence. A Results passage reports n=20 while Methods reports 21. The paper describes a pair-level split with 34 training pairs and pairs 35–40 for validation/evaluation, but the reviewed article does not establish that individual birds are disjoint across pairs. The response window is an operational timing rule, not a semantic label. The separate Zenodo data record (23047646) lists four raw example tracks plus processed-data and detector archives, not a verified copy of the full study corpus. Its API license field says CC BY-SA 4.0 while its description says the data are CC BY-NC; this conflict leaves reuse unresolved. The separate 26.6 GB code/model ZIP (23024019) remains opaque at the internal-file level. Supplemental analyses and independent reanalysis were not reviewed.
lesson: Sequence models can learn who tends to vocalize next, when a call occurs and how acoustic features covary. That is a valuable first step for animal communication research, but prediction is not translation. Start with measurable acoustic patterns and independently observed context; require held-out-animal tests and a human review path. Do not turn the controlled playback experiment into a feature of Talk2Nature's passive app.
next_review: Keep both Zenodo records metadata-only. Before considering any reuse, resolve the contradictory CC BY-SA versus CC BY-NC terms for record 23047646 and identify which exact data files the license covers; only then consider a bounded inspection. Resolve the 20-versus-21 bird count and whether train/evaluation pairs share individuals, and obtain independent avian-communication and ML/evaluation review. No archive acquisition, model run or playback is proposed by this note.
expert_review: No independent specialist review has been received.

Next-caller accuracy 0.632 vs 0.496 chance; next-token accuracy 0.056 vs 0.010; wait-time RMSE 976 s vs 1,126.4 s for a random-distribution baseline. These are task-specific preprint results, not semantic accuracy.
34 pairs used for training and pairs 35–40 for validation/evaluation; disjointness of individual birds across pairs is not established in the reviewed text.

title: Zebra finches categorize call types; translation remains a bigger question
seo_description: A study already compares zebra-finch behavioral and acoustic-call confusions; a modern audio-model extension still needs exact data matching.
review_stage: Peer-reviewed article text and public release metadata reviewed; archive contents and analyses not reproduced
review_depth: Reviewed the full PMC-indexed article text, including the abstract, reported results, Figure 4 caption and data statement on October 24; the UC Berkeley institutional-copy record; the authors' public GitHub README/root listing; and the 2026 BirdAVES article. On October 25, refreshed official Figshare v1 and Zenodo v1/v3 API metadata over verified TLS, including current file inventories, provider checksums and record-level license declarations. The Figshare landing-page description exposes a filename convention and warns of known naming discrepancies. No Figshare or Zenodo payload, article supplement, audio, source code or model weights were downloaded or reproduced; the new publisher search extract was used only to confirm the 2026 article's title, framing and reported result excerpt.
review_locator: Elie et al., Science 389(6766):1210–1215 (2025), DOI 10.1126/science.ads8482. PMC article: PMC12721838. Figshare audio record: DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11905533.v1. The final PMC article data statement cites versioned Zenodo record 13623969 (v1); the UC Berkeley copy cites concept DOI 13623968, whose later v3 resubmission is record 15795568 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15795568). This resolves the citation targets, but not which release files support the final published analyses.
finding: The paper reports that 12 adult zebra finches learned to discriminate all 11 researcher-defined call types in an operant Go/No-Go task. The stimuli came from a library described as more than 8,000 call renditions by 45 vocalizers, and birds generalized to unfamiliar renditions. The paper already compares acoustic-classifier confusion with behavioral confusion and reports more errors among call types used in similar behavioral contexts than its acoustic-similarity comparison predicted. The authors' README describes the spectrogram classifier matrices as leave-one-vocalizer-out LDA results. Thus basic model-versus-bird confusion alignment is published prior art. A separate 2026 article applies BirdAVES to supplied call labels, but the reviewed article does not directly compare those modern-model errors with the measured behavioral confusion matrix.
limitations: The task was trained, closed-set discrimination of human-defined call categories, not spontaneous conversation, receiver behavior in a natural exchange or open-ended translation. The behavioral and acoustic confusion matrices are described at call-category level, so a matrix-level reproduction may not require a one-to-one audio-to-trial join if the exact published matrices are present in a rights-cleared release. A new raw-audio representation comparison does require matching audio files to call labels, vocalizer identities and the same stimulus population. The Figshare record lists 3,433 WAV files, some containing sequences; their mapping to the paper's more than 8,000 renditions and to the 2026 classifier inputs is unverified. The final Science paper links the versioned v1 record 13623969; the Berkeley copy cites concept DOI 13623968, whose later v3 release is record 15795568. This citation resolution does not establish which archive files support the final published analyses; archive contents and component-level rights remain unresolved. Figshare and Zenodo declare CC BY 4.0 at record level, while the GitHub repository displays no license file. The Figshare landing-page description gives the filename pattern ColColxxxx_yymmdd-VT-zz.wav, which appears to encode vocalizer, date, vocalization type and rendition, but it warns that naming discrepancies are known. Its current API manifest lists two ZIP files and a notes PDF, without per-file MD5 values; the page text says the archives contain 3,433 WAVs. These are possible join keys, not a verified mapping to the 2025 stimulus set. Zenodo's current v1 and v3 API records report provider MD5 values, but archive contents were not retrieved and those checksums were not verified locally.
lesson: Zebra finch remains an evidence-grounded perception-methods lead, but both core comparison ingredients are prior art: Elie et al. (2025) compare an acoustic LDA confusion matrix with measured finch discrimination, and Radočaj & Radočaj (2026) already use behavior-derived functional categories as auxiliary targets for a frozen-BirdAVES multi-task classifier. A distinct extension could ask whether model errors align with the measured receiver-confusion matrix on matched held-out vocalizers, beyond the published LDA and acoustic-similarity baselines. That remains conditional on a defensible audio/call/vocalizer crosswalk, exact component rights and independent review; even a positive result would concern trained discrimination, not translation.
next_review: Keep all files metadata-only. The official Figshare filename pattern and the Zenodo v1/v3 metadata are now recorded, but neither pattern nor provider checksum verifies archive contents or an audio-to-trial join. Before considering any permitted archive inspection, ask independent avian-perception and ML/statistical reviewers whether a matched receiver-confusion comparison adds value beyond the 2025 LDA comparison and 2026 biologically informed multi-task model. If they support it, define the minimum files and rights review first; otherwise defer. Do not acquire data, code or model weights or run a model until those gates pass.

title: A zebra-finch classifier is a baseline, not a translator
seo_description: A 2026 zebra-finch study classifies call labels with BirdAVES. One split and unresolved dataset counts leave key reproduction questions.
year_label: Peer-reviewed Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction article
review_stage: Publisher article review plus current indexed claim check; metadata refreshed; no reproduction
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher-hosted article's abstract, data/methods, bird-level partition, evaluation, results, limitations, conclusion and data statement on October 24, plus the article-specific version history and AVEX documentation. On October 25, rechecked the publisher-indexed title, framing and result excerpt; the direct MDPI page returned HTTP 429 during this refresh, so no new full-text review is claimed. The official Figshare v1 and Zenodo v1/v3 APIs were refreshed over verified TLS. No archive, code, audio or BirdAVES weights were acquired or run, and no model result was reproduced.
review_locator: Radočaj & Radočaj, ‘Biologically Informed Multi-Task Learning for Call-Type Classification in Zebra Finches Using Functional Semantic Hierarchies,’ Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction 8(10), 318 (2026), DOI 10.3390/make8100318. Dataset record: Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11905533.v1. Earlier repertoire study: Elie & Theunissen, Animal Cognition 19 (2016), DOI 10.1007/s10071-015-0933-6. Model documentation: Earth Species Project AVES/BirdAVES repository.
finding: The 2026 article introduces multi-task classification using frozen BirdAVES embeddings: it predicts 11 supplied call-type labels and six behavior-derived functional/semantic categories as an auxiliary target. The authors report a best call-type result of 87.11% accuracy and 82.76% macro-F1, versus 84.86% and 78.89% for their single-task call-type baseline. They report one predefined 70:15:15 split by bird. These are author-reported results, not reproduced by Talk2Nature. The semantic categories are supervised labels from an existing taxonomy; they are not discovered meanings or an open-ended translation.
limitations: The paper says 50 birds, while Elie & Theunissen (2016) report 45 birds and 8,136 segmented calls from 3,405 bouts; the Figshare record lists 3,433 WAV files. The 2026 paper says each input is a single isolated vocalization, whereas the Figshare record warns that files may contain a vocalization or sequence. These may reflect different processing or dataset versions, but the relationship and unitization are unresolved. The evaluation uses one split; only 3 DistressCall recordings appear in its test partition. The colony recordings do not establish performance on ordinary homes or field soundscapes. The study does not test receiver responses or align model errors with the 2025 behavioral-trial confusion data. Exact BirdAVES variant, weight terms, article authors’ experiment-code location and supplementary contents remain unresolved. AVEX declares MIT for its library code, which is a separate component and does not license pretrained weights or data. Dataset, article, code and model-weight rights are separate; the dataset record declares CC BY 4.0, the journal specifies CC BY 4.0 for the article, and no data/model asset has been cleared or admitted. This study is important prior art for using a behavior-derived semantic hierarchy as model supervision. It does not report a direct item-level comparison between its predictions and the receiver birds' measured confusion responses from the 2025 experiment.
lesson: Call-type prediction and behavior-informed multi-task training are both published prior art. A separate research question could test whether a modern model's call-type error structure aligns with measured receiver confusions on the same verified stimuli and unseen vocalizers, beyond the 2025 LDA/acoustic-similarity comparison. This requires an exact audio-to-call/vocalizer crosswalk, rights for each component, a selected model variant, independent avian and ML/statistical review, and a locked evaluation. It would measure correspondence with a learned discrimination task, not translation.
next_review: Keep metadata-only. The filename pattern reported by Figshare may support a future crosswalk, but known naming discrepancies and the 3,433-file/50-bird versus 45-vocalizer/8,000-rendition descriptions remain unresolved. Obtain independent review of whether direct receiver-confusion alignment adds value beyond the 2025 LDA comparison and this 2026 semantically informed multi-task model. If the question is retained, first resolve exact BirdAVES variant and weight terms, the published partition and source-file join, model/data overlap, and component rights. Do not acquire payloads or run models before that decision and protocol are reviewed.

title: A global bird-song study finds shared acoustic patterns—not a universal bird language
seo_description: A 2026 Science study analyzed 116,792 song bouts from 3,160 passerine species. Here is what large-scale acoustic analysis can—and cannot—tell us.
review_stage: PubMed abstract, authors’ public repository README and pinned tree metadata, GBIF metadata, five public Xeno-canto record-page license examples, and official API documentation reviewed; full article methods, supplement and full recording-level study inventory not reviewed; no file payloads or code acquired or run
review_depth: The PubMed abstract reports an analysis of acoustic song architecture across more than 3,000 passerine species and eight recurring motifs associated with species traits and sound-propagation conditions. The authors’ repository README identifies 116,792 song bouts from 3,160 species, describes modulation-power-spectrum features and lists analysis scripts and derived-data files. finding: This is a strong example of large citizen-science sound collections enabling a useful cross-species analysis. The paper reports eight recurring acoustic motifs in songs from thousands of passerine species and associations between motif distributions, species traits and sound-propagation conditions. The author repository describes a 37-dimensional acoustic feature space built from modulation power spectra and unsupervised clustering. This is evidence about acoustic form and broad ecological patterns; the reviewed sources do not establish call meanings, receiver comprehension or a general bird-to-human language model.
limitations: The study's apparent scale does not make its recordings a single rights-cleared training set. The pinned Git tree contains 1,280 audio-segment files (185,758,300 provider-reported bytes), not 1,280 verified independent recordings; the metadata payload and filename-to-source joins were not inspected. The GBIF record is a metadata distribution subset with its own CC BY-NC 4.0 declaration; it is not a blanket license for underlying audio. Xeno-canto recording pages display item-level terms, illustrated by CC BY-NC-ND 2.5 and CC BY-SA 4.0 examples, and the exact study-recording membership and each source license were not checked. The author repository README states CC BY 4.0, but the tree has no standalone LICENSE file and the README does not resolve the license scope for code, derived tables, maps and third-party audio. Its Zenodo DOI remains a placeholder. The paper methods, exact source IDs, quality-control rules, annotations, class balance, split design, geographic/recordist sampling and full license chain remain unaudited. This analysis is prior art for global passerine acoustic motifs, not a new Talk2Nature result or a semantic-communication benchmark. The filename screen yields 495 numeric-ID candidates, but only three were spot-checked and only one filename/taxon pair matched; it does not prove all filenames map to source recordings or that any sample belongs to the paper's analyzed set. Sample license terms vary (two CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, one CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Official API access requires a key and is rate-limited; no full metadata/license census is available.
lesson: Large shared sound archives can reveal repeatable acoustic patterns across many species. To study communication, pair sound with careful, independent observations of what animals and receivers do, preserve uncertainty and test generalization across animals and settings. Scale is valuable only when labels, provenance, licensing and evaluation match the question.

title: Synchronized finch recordings help locate calls, not translate them
seo_description: BirdPark links zebra-finch audio, video and body-vibration sensors. The data can inform vocal-event and caller-labeling methods, not call meaning.
year_label: Peer-reviewed system paper; related dataset records span 2024–2026
review_stage: Paper abstract and selected searchable methods passages plus exact dataset-record metadata reviewed; no dataset, code or model acquired or run
review_depth: Reviewed the PubMed bibliographic record and abstract, searchable PMC passages on shared-clock synchronization, multimodal vocal segmentation and channel-miss evaluation, the ETH Research Collection article-rights record, and exact Zenodo v2 descriptions and file inventories for records 13144875 and 20608098. The ETH Zurich dataset record was reviewed for its description and rights label. The complete paper, supplement, annotation guides, CSV contents, audio/video/accelerometer files, code and model weights were not inspected or acquired. No independent avian or ML/statistical reviewer assessed this note.
review_locator: Rüttimann et al. (2025), PeerJ 13:e20203, DOI 10.7717/peerj.20203; Zenodo v2 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.13144875; Zenodo v2 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20608098; ETH Zurich dataset DOI 10.3929/ethz-c-000788603.
finding: BirdPark is a specialized synchronized recording system combining video, stationary microphones and animal-borne accelerometer transmitters. The paper uses redundant channels to help find vocal events and separate likely caller sources in freely behaving zebra-finch groups. The public records describe several related but distinct releases: a Zenodo v2 record claiming 112 minutes across four experiments, a later annotator-training pack with a 4.5 GB pair-example archive, and an ETH record describing ten mixed-sex pairs (20 birds) with annotated clean and overlapping vocalizations. These resources could inform bounded vocal-event, overlap and caller-attribution methods. Their labels do not establish what a call means or whether a bird understood a message.
limitations: The article's searched Table 2 passage describes a 28-minute segmentation evaluation slice, while Zenodo v2 describes 112 minutes across four experiments; the relationship and exact common sample coverage were not reconciled, so these counts must not be combined. The Zenodo records show no dataset license field; the ETH record says In Copyright - Non-Commercial Use Permitted, which does not clear commercial training or redistribution. The separate releases may overlap and are not independent cohorts by default. The recording setup is a specialized lab system with microphones, cameras and body-worn sensors, not an ordinary phone workflow. The inspected labels concern event boundaries, signal visibility or source attribution, not independently established call meaning, receiver response or open-ended communication. Split membership, annotator agreement and component provenance remain unreviewed.
next_review: Keep each dataset metadata-only. First reconcile the paper-to-deposit relationship, exact recording and annotation coverage, and rights for each component; do not retrieve payloads while dataset terms are absent or restrictive. Ask an independent avian-bioacoustics and ML/statistical reviewer whether a small, animal-held-out vocal-event or caller-attribution task is useful and whether the available annotations support it. If rights or independent units do not support a defensible test, retain BirdPark as a methods reference and keep zebra-finch behavioral categorization as a separate literature lead. Do not present this work as a meaning benchmark or use animal playback.
lesson: Synchronized audio and video can help establish when an animal vocalized and which source may have produced the sound. That is a useful step toward studying interactions, but caller attribution and event segmentation are not evidence that a model understands the call.
study_snapshot: The article describes a central timing source synchronizing microphones, cameras and body-borne accelerometer transmitters; a custom animal lab setup supplied redundant views of vocal activity.

These are candidate resources for segmentation and source attribution. Neither the paper nor the reviewed deposits provide a ground-truth label for what a call means to a receiver.

title: Human-guided clustering helps label zebra-finch calls, not decode meaning
seo_description: A 2026 zebra-finch study found human-guided acoustic clustering approached expert agreement, but tested neither call meaning nor new birds.
review_depth: Reviewed the full 15-page article text, including methods, reported ARI/NMI results, time comparison, split design, discussion, acknowledgments and data statement. Queried exact Zenodo record and version APIs for 18156254, 22657329 and 18100613; read the pinned GitHub README, root requirements and MIT license; and compared the exact WhisperSeg model page with pinned revision metadata. No data archive, code, model weights or supplement was downloaded or executed. Figures were not visually reanalyzed and no independent specialist reviewed this note.
review_stage: Full article and source metadata reviewed; no reproduction or third-party payload acquisition
review_locator: Lee, K., Basha, M., Zai, A. T. & Hahnloser, R. H. R. (2026). Benchmarking Automated and Semi-Automated Vocal Clustering Methods. Applied Sciences 16(2), 810. DOI 10.3390/app16020810. Dataset DOI cited by paper: 10.5281/zenodo.18156254; newer version: 10.5281/zenodo.22657329.
finding: The article reports 1,454 randomly selected 44.1 kHz vocalizations from three isolated zebra finches recorded between 55 and 136 days post-hatch, with independent manual clusters from three experts for each bird. Mean ARI/NMI were 0.78/0.83 for expert-to-expert manual agreement, 0.73/0.81 for human-refined clusters and 0.62/0.71 for fully automated Whisper-based clustering. The authors also report about 90 minutes per bird for manual clustering versus 45 minutes for semi-automated proofreading. These are published results, not Talk2Nature reproductions. The method suggests that model proposals plus human correction may scale annotation while preserving expert review; its categories are acoustic clusters, not validated call meanings.
limitations: The article's 80/20 split randomly holds out vocalizations within each bird-and-annotator combination and evaluates nine such combinations from only three birds; it does not test unseen-bird or cross-species generalization. The study analyzes acoustic similarity rather than receiver response, social context or semantics. Time savings and agreement were reported on this small task, not independently verified. The Zenodo API shows that paper-cited v1 record 18156254 and v2 record 22657329 share conceptrecid 18156253, with different archive sizes and checksums. The v2 record note also names 18100613 as an earlier publication, but that DOI has a different conceptrecid (18100612); its relationship to the article data is unresolved. The Zenodo APIs declare CC BY 4.0, but the paper acknowledges permission to use a subset from an external dataset, so source-audio rights and exact archive contents require reconciliation. The code repository is MIT at the pinned revision. The model card displays Apache-2.0 for WhisperSeg, while the pinned model API reports no license value; the paper's Whisper embedding model revision is not identified. No independent reviewer or reproduction exists.
lesson: A useful Talk2Nature tool could let a model suggest acoustically similar clips while a person accepts, splits, merges, tags as uncertain or leaves them unclassified. Suggestions and human labels must remain separate and reviewable. The interface can simplify the task for new contributors while preserving an advanced expert view, annotation provenance and disagreement. UMAP clusters or acoustic embeddings must not be presented as behavioral categories or translations.
next_review: First reconcile the Zenodo version chain, exact 1,454-item manifest and external source-audio permission with the authors' declarations. Preserve the article, dataset, repository code, WhisperSeg checkpoint and Whisper embedding weights as separate assets. Ask independent bioacoustics and ML/statistical reviewers whether a new annotation-efficiency or agreement question is useful beyond the published study. If rights and review gates pass, specify a bounded human task and hold out whole birds for any generalization claim; no training, data import or product integration is authorized by this note.
expert_review: No independent avian-bioacoustics, animal-welfare, human-factors or ML/statistical review has been completed.

title: Cross-species pitch benchmark helps estimate vocal pitch, not meaning
seo_description: A 2025 cross-species dataset benchmarks vocal pitch contours across mammals and birds; its monk-parakeet results do not decode meaning.
taxon: Multiple mammals and birds; monk parakeet subset
review_depth: Reviewed the full 2025 PMC article, Dryad landing page and official dataset/version/file-manifest APIs, Dryad reuse guidance, and the pinned code tree. For source lineage, reviewed the 2025 paper's monk-parakeet table/references, the 2021 Animal Behaviour publisher abstract/data-accessibility statement and Figshare API manifest, plus the 2023 PLOS article record, Figshare v2 API and streamed README. The Dryad API snapshot is saved in research/dryad_f0_manifest_2026-10-24.json. No Dryad archive, audio, selection-table payload, code or weights were acquired or run; no Figshare rows or KML contents were inspected.
review_stage: Full-text article and source metadata reviewed; metadata-only, with no reproduction or specialist review
review_locator: Best et al. (2025), Bioacoustics 34(4), 419–446, DOI 10.1080/09524622.2025.2500380; Dryad DOI 10.5061/dryad.prr4xgxw8; Smith-Vidaurre et al. (2021), Animal Behaviour 179, 15–39, DOI 10.1016/j.anbehav.2021.06.020 and Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.14811636.v1; Smith-Vidaurre et al. (2023), PLOS Computational Biology 19(7), e1011231 and Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.22582099.v2.
finding: The article reports 250,670 calls from 14 taxa with annotated fundamental-frequency (F0) contours. The Dryad release lists waveforms and annotations for 13 taxa; it also includes F0 predictions for bottlenose dolphins whose waveforms could not be published. The listed release totals 27.86 GB. Rodents contribute 224,705/250,670 calls (about 89.6%), while monk parakeets contribute 233. In the paper’s target-trained CREPE comparison, monk-parakeet pitch accuracy is 0.30 under that study’s half-semitone metric. This is an acoustic-feature estimation score, not a communication or meaning score. The 2025 paper cites Smith-Vidaurre et al. (2021, 2023) papers and deposits as sources for the 233 semi-automatically annotated monk-parakeet calls. The 2021 Figshare record lists 12 CSV/KML/README files and no waveform. The 2023 Figshare v2 inventory lists a 440,873-byte selection table and a 31,079,669-byte WAV archive; its README says their sound.file names correspond across those files and reports 1,596 calls in the table, 1,582 used in the paper. This offers a possible metadata-only source-file comparison, but the exact mapping of the F0 paper's 233 calls to the 2023 files remains unverified. The Dryad API v9 manifest lists 15 files totaling 27,863,357,661 bytes and identifies monk_parakeets.zip as 5,076,570 bytes with a provider-reported SHA-256. This is inventory metadata only: the archive and its file_list.txt have not been downloaded or inspected, and the checksum has not been recomputed locally.
limitations: The benchmark targets a single F0 contour and discards overlapping sections; it does not label call category, behavioral context, addressee, receiver response or meaning. It is highly imbalanced by taxon, combines manual, semi-automatic and automatic annotation procedures, and model performance varies with signal characteristics. The 14-taxa article count and 13-taxa waveform deposit differ because dolphin predictions are present without the dolphin waveforms. The paper, data, code and weights have separate reuse terms. The exact source-recording provenance and independent-unit split structure were not reconciled in this review. The pinned 75-entry GitHub tree has no LICENSE/COPYING file; code and checkpoint terms remain unresolved. The 2025 article's main text does not give a call-to-file crosswalk. No archive or selection-table payload was downloaded, rows and KML contents were not inspected, and provider checksums were not recomputed locally. The 2023 README's file-name relationship is a lead, not a verified match to the F0 subset; source-recording provenance and location sensitivity remain open. The official Dryad file-download API returned an authorization requirement and the public file-stream route returned HTTP 403 in this environment; no archive member names or audio were inspected.
lesson: This is a useful candidate for testing whether an acoustic pipeline can estimate a measurable feature such as pitch on non-human calls. It could support a carefully bounded feature benchmark after rights, provenance and grouping checks. It cannot train or validate a system that claims to understand what an animal said. Keep the 233-call monk-parakeet subset distinct from much larger taxa and report per-taxon results rather than a pooled headline score.
next_review: The API manifest fixes the current Dryad version and provider checksum, but retrieving the archive through the documented route requires bearer authentication and the public file-stream route returned HTTP 403 in this environment. Do not bypass collector limits or use an unapproved credential. If a documented public route to the metadata-only file_list becomes available, compare it with the 2023 selection-table sound.file values without inspecting audio or location fields; otherwise keep the 233-call subset metadata-only. Any later file-level work must confirm individual/session/source-study keys and location sensitivity, freeze a group-held-out pitch-tracking evaluation, and obtain independent bioacoustics and ML/statistical review before acquisition or model execution.

title: A large insect sound dataset can test species recognition—not what a call means
seo_description: InsectSet459 contains 26,298 recordings from 459 insect species. What its labels and frequency range can—and cannot—teach an animal-listening app.
review_stage: PubMed primary abstract, official Zenodo v1.1 description and file list, and author repository root/README reviewed; full article methods and annotation CSV contents not reviewed; no media, code or model acquired or run
review_depth: The paper abstract reports 26,298 recordings (226.6 hours) from 459 Orthoptera and Cicadidae species. The Zenodo v1.1 record lists an 83.7 GB package, including a 6.9 MB annotation CSV, and describes source recordings as CC licenses 4.0 or CC0. The record states a 60/20/20 split balanced by file number and duration. The paper describes broad recording sample rates, from 8 to 500 kHz. Approximately one third of files use sample rates above 44 kHz according to the paper. The full paper methods, split membership, original annotation rows, source-level license manifest, location values and code were not inspected.
review_locator: Faiß, Ghani and Stowell (2026), Scientific Data 13:499, DOI 10.1038/s41597-026-07123-4; Zenodo v1.1 DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18554693.
finding: InsectSet459 is a substantial, multi-species resource for insect sound identification and testing audio pipelines across varied sample rates. Its species labels do not identify behavior, caller intent, receiver response or message meaning. The recording diversity also means a phone microphone should not be assumed to capture every insect signal; high-frequency work may need a separately validated sensor.
limitations: The dataset is weakly labeled at the recording level, and its published split is described as balanced by files and audio duration rather than as a held-out contributor, locality or device evaluation. The full test archive and annotations are published, so this is not a secret locked test set. The 6.9 MB annotation CSV exceeds Talk2Nature’s 5 MiB per-file collection limit; the 83.7 GB archive is not a bounded acquisition. The dataset description lists CC 4.0 or CC0 source recordings, but exact source-level terms and attributions still need to be retained for any selected file. The linked curation-code repository has no located standalone license. No Talk2Nature reproduction, hardware test or insect-behavior review has been performed.
lesson: This is a useful engineering reference for a future insect-sound identification track and for explaining why different taxa may need different microphones. It is not a first communication benchmark and does not validate phone capture or a universal animal-listening app.
next_review: Keep the v1.1 record metadata-only. Do not fetch the annotation CSV by splitting it around the collector limit or download the full archive. title: Which companion animal is ready for a first study?
seo_description: A source-based comparison of cat, dog and parrot datasets separates household-app fit from evidence that can support a scientific benchmark.
review_stage: Synthesis of existing source-linked records; no new data, code or model inspected
review_depth: Compared the existing full-paper review of dog-bark classification; CatMeows record and rights metadata; full-text review and deposit metadata for two companion-parrot surveys; primary methods and official deposit inventory for budgerigar vocal/sociality data; and the publisher abstract for a 2026 edge-monitoring study. Supporting survey workbooks and third-party media were not acquired or inspected. This is a library-bounded comparison, not a systematic review or independent specialist assessment.
finding: Among the reviewed resources, no public companion-animal corpus combines naturally occurring household audio, independently time-aligned behavior or receiver-response labels, verified household/individual/session grouping, and fully reviewed reuse terms. CatMeows describes 440 sounds from 21 cats with context and owner/session identifiers, but its CC BY-NC 4.0 terms do not provide general commercial permission and the contexts are elicited. A dog-bark paper analyzes 16,789 segments from 74 dogs during designed home exposures; its reported classifier predicts associations with those situations, not what dogs mean. Parrot surveys describe caregiver reports about human-language mimicry and names, not an acoustic training corpus. A budgerigar research deposit contains derived call features and separate social observations without source call WAVs or event-aligned behavior; a separate 2026 abstract reports local vocal-activity monitoring, not a conversation model.
limitations: The comparison covers only the named, already reviewed records and cannot establish that no other suitable dataset exists. Reported record counts are not independent sample counts. Dog contexts were linked to designed stimuli, CatMeows files were not acquired, parrot questionnaire workbooks were not inspected, and the budgerigar edge paper's full methods were unavailable in this review. No files, recordings, labels, code or weights were acquired or run; no animal-carer interviews or independent scientific review occurred.
lesson: Keep two decisions separate. For a household Field Companion, use a species-neutral observation workflow and keep budgerigars as a provisional usability cohort only if genuine carer access and qualified avian input emerge. For a data-based ML exercise, select a narrow outcome from a corpus with suitable source files, independent labels, grouping keys and rights; a larger dataset does not make it a communication benchmark. Preserve the observer's account, recorded signal, reviewed behavior and model prediction as separate evidence.
next_review: Ask an independent avian/bioacoustics and ML/statistical reviewer to challenge the existing first-dataset decision packet. Before selecting a household cohort, establish access to multiple willing carers and qualified species-specific advice; test the interface with synthetic sessions first. Do not recruit, collect or upload real observations under this literature comparison.
expert_review: Not independently reviewed by a comparative animal-behavior, companion-animal or bioacoustics specialist.
study_snapshot: CatMeows records 440 sounds from 21 cats with context and owner/session identifiers; elicited contexts and CC BY-NC 4.0 terms limit transfer to a commercial app. Files remain unacquired.

The reviewed bark-classification paper reports 74 dogs and 16,789 segments from designed home exposures. Its selected task predicts stimulus-associated labels; the paper-described dataset has no public versioned deposit in the reviewed record.

Two owner surveys describe reported phrase use across many companion-parrot species. They inform observation-interface design, but are not audio corpora or independent receiver-response tests; supporting workbooks remain uninspected.

A public vocal/social deposit has derived features and separate social observations but no source call WAVs or shared event timestamps. A separate early-access study describes vocal-activity monitoring, not semantic interpretation.
Budgerigars remain a provisional household usability cohort; no companion species is selected as a training-ready communication benchmark.

title: Honeybee dance records connect movement with followers and food sites
seo_description: Honeybee dance data link waggle signals with followers and feeder outcomes. A bounded communication study, not a general animal translator.
review_depth: Targeted review of the PNAS Nexus abstract, communication background, colony and camera setup, annotation and hourly sample grouping, follower/feeder results, data statement and article license; on 2026-10-25, rechecked the complete Zenodo v1.0 API file manifest and dataset license. The 11 listed sizes sum to 4,870,358,178 bytes; the named follower CSV is 9,171,824 bytes. No data, video, code or model was downloaded, locally hashed, inspected or executed.
finding: Dormagen et al. combined waggle-phase detection, individual tracking, follower observations and feeder records. The paper reports more than 100,000 detected waggle phases. A manually annotated subset covers 176 videos, 3,278,121 detections from 28,873 tracks and 4,389 bee IDs, including 1,107 waggle phases and 279 follower events. The Zenodo v1.0 API lists 11 deposited files totaling 4,870,358,178 bytes (4.87 decimal GB), alongside more than 46 million 2019 track detections. This is a rare data path connecting a well-defined sender signal to observed receiver behavior and known food-site outcomes.
limitations: This is not a blank slate: the paper already analyzes waggle dance/follower relationships and feeder outcomes. It spans one observation-hive site across two seasons; the published sample-level cross-validation groups by hour rather than holding out bees or colonies. The 2021 recordings lack marked individual identities. The dataset is specialized tracking and video data, not an ordinary-phone audio corpus. The public record contains fine-scale feeder coordinates, which are not reproduced here. The separately named Berlin2019_followers.csv is 9,171,824 bytes, above the current 5 MiB per-file collector cap; smaller dance/feeder metadata files have not been shown to substitute for the follower outcome. No payload bytes were inspected. CC BY 4.0 in the Zenodo API covers the deposit, not linked software or model artifacts.
lesson: A useful communication study needs a defined signal, an observed receiver response and an independent outcome. Honeybees are a strong candidate for testing that chain, while existing claims and the single-site scope demand a narrow, independently reviewed question. This does not justify a general language model or claim that unknown animal speech has been translated.
next_review: Ask independent insect-behavior and ML/statistical reviewers whether any non-duplicative question remains and whether the relevant files support a bee-held-out evaluation. Any future follower-file intake needs a separately reviewed path that respects the 5 MiB per-file limit; do not bypass it with direct downloads, alternate tools or archive splitting. Keep fine-scale location metadata out of public outputs. No payload acquisition or model run is authorized by this note.

title: MooLogue separates cattle-call learning from live analysis
seo_description: A published cattle-vocalization app offers a mobile learning precedent. Its paper, repository and restricted dataset have different versions and rights.
kind: Mobile app, curated audio library and machine-learning workflow review
review_stage: Targeted article and pinned-repository review; metadata-only, no reproduction
review_depth: Reviewed selected abstract, app design and release, curated-corpus description, dataset-access statement and article license in an author-uploaded article copy. Read the README and README_softwarex.md at pinned GitHub commit 8023dbdfed8587d07eeafa54accb68408ffaefbe. The Zenodo API metadata request returned HTTP 406, so its manifest was not independently inspected. No app was installed, no repository archive or dataset payload was acquired, and no code or model was run.
finding: Kate and Neethirajan describe MooLogue as a Flutter mobile application for learning about cattle vocalizations. The paper reports a curated library built from 569 clips, 48 fine-grained behavioral classes and three commercial dairy farms, grouped into nine high-level learning categories. Its published v1.0 is described as an offline-first educational app with curated examples and metadata bundled for normal use. The pinned public repository README instead describes a cloud workflow that uploads recordings to AWS, runs PyTorch inference and returns a label, confidence and recommended action. The repository snapshot is dated 2025-11-25, and the paper does not establish that this exact snapshot is the implementation of the later v1.0. Treat the discrepancy as unresolved. This is a useful mobile-learning and version-control case study, not evidence that an app can translate cattle calls or provide validated welfare advice.
limitations: The article was reviewed selectively from an author-uploaded copy, not in full through the publisher; figures and supplemental artifacts were not inspected. The paper says the audio and metadata are restricted under a data access agreement to protect farm confidentiality; the direct Zenodo API request failed, and no item manifest or file-level terms were checked. The pinned GitHub tree has no root LICENSE file although its README metadata says MIT and GitHub reports no detected license. No exact mapping from that 2025 source snapshot to the 2026 published app release was established. No app store installation, source build, upload, classifier, model weights or welfare recommendation was tested. The app paper is not an independent usability study or proof of interpretive accuracy, and the project does not validate open-ended communication or generalization to other farms/species.
lesson: Separate human-facing education, user-started observation, automated prediction and any care recommendation into distinct product claims and data flows. A curated listen-and-learn mode can be useful without claiming live translation. For Talk2Nature, keep raw capture local by default until consent, data rights, storage, withdrawal and review are resolved; present model outputs as uncertain predictions with provenance, never as animal intent or treatment advice.
next_review: Reconcile the exact published app version with a versioned source release and a real code license before considering reuse. Independently inspect current app-store behavior and privacy terms only if a specific product comparison needs them. Keep the restricted dataset metadata-only; do not request access, download media or reuse model assets without a defined protocol, permission and component-specific rights review. Obtain independent cattle-welfare/bioacoustics and ML review before making any accuracy or welfare claim.

title: Nocturnal bird migration data localizes calls, not communication meaning
seo_description: A source-based review of the NBM nocturnal bird dataset: fine time-frequency call labels, a detection baseline, and separate data and model rights.
review_stage: Publisher methods/evaluation and official record metadata reviewed; data, code and weights remain unacquired
review_depth: Reviewed the Scientific Data article's abstract, methods, data records, technical validation, model-evaluation description, data/code availability and article-rights statement; the current Zenodo v4 landing page and file list; the linked GitHub repository root and README; and the Zenodo software-record page. No dataset file, metadata CSV, audio, code archive or model weight was downloaded, opened, installed or executed. No result was independently reproduced.
finding: The NBM resource is a useful example of volunteer-supported passive-acoustic annotation for a narrow bird-monitoring task. Its training collection is reported as 2,077 audio files, 13,359 time-and-frequency vocalization annotations, about 38 hours and 117 species; 883 training files came from Xeno-Canto. The paper reports a two-stage object detector and mAP@IoU0.5 of 0.67 on 45 species. Those outputs localize and classify calls on spectrograms. They do not label observed behavior, receiver response, intention or meaning. The paper's test-set description says six XC files per species, 270 total, selected from recordings uploaded after the training collection; its detection-evaluation section instead says 271 recordings. Resolve that one-file discrepancy before attempting reproduction.
limitations: The upload-time cutoff does not by itself establish separation by bird, recording site, uploader or other biological grouping. The baseline is author-reported and not independently reproduced. The article's comparison with BirdNET includes a different multi-label classification task, so scores should not be treated as a direct translation comparison. Zenodo states that NBM-Orig audio is CC BY 4.0 while XC-origin recordings keep their individual licenses; it also describes date/location metadata for almost all XC files. Annotation and metadata terms need separate confirmation, and any future location handling must minimize precise wildlife sites. The GitHub README points to Zenodo v3 (DOI 17544346) while the paper and current dataset record point to v4 (DOI 17573913). The repository displays a model_weights folder, but no license file was visible in the inspected root; the linked 128 MB software record's license field and archive contents were not verified. Code, weights, paper text, recordings and metadata therefore remain separate rights questions.
lesson: Fine time-frequency labels make NBM a strong methods reference for event localization, volunteer annotation quality checks and model evaluation. It is not the Talk2Nature first communication benchmark and does not change the provisional Great Tit song-structure, honeybee receiver-observation, bat context-prediction or companion-budgerigar paths. It does reveal a practical product gap: Talk2Nature's current time-only observation exports cannot represent a frequency-bounded call. Treat a spectrogram annotation mode as a future researcher need to validate, not an automatic feature request. Keep species identity, acoustic event, observed context and receiver behavior as distinct data fields.
next_review: If a researcher proposes using NBM as an event-detection methods baseline, reconcile the 270/271 test count, pin the exact v4 files, inspect per-recording provenance and location fields without publishing sensitive coordinates, and confirm annotation/metadata rights. Review the pinned code and checkpoint licenses and source version separately. Require a reviewer-approved recording/site/uploader grouping plan and independent reproduction before comparing results. Until then retain metadata only; do not acquire, run or train on these materials.

title: BirdNET Live keeps bird identification on the phone
seo_description: A source-based review of BirdNET Live v1.2.1: local bird-species detection, session export, opt-in network services and separate code/model licenses.
kind: Mobile app, privacy and model-rights review
review_stage: Official app documentation/privacy policy and pinned GitHub release reviewed; no app install, model execution or independent validation
review_depth: Reviewed official Getting Started and Privacy pages (policy updated 2026-08-06) plus the GitHub v1.2.1 release at commit 4aee47cd824873ffc9b3ca3462bf2415151a56d1, including README, LICENSE and MODEL_LICENSE. Documentation describes app flows and developer data-handling claims; these were not independently runtime-tested. No app, source archive, model, audio or training data was acquired or run.
finding: BirdNET Live is an open-source Flutter app for Android and iOS, with Windows described as experimental. The v1.2.1 release identifies bird species from sound using on-device BirdNET+ inference; the README describes 9,789 species, Live/Point Count/Survey/File Analysis/ARU modes, reviewable sessions and local exports. The official privacy policy says the app has no backend and does not send audio to external servers. The Getting Started guide says microphone permission is required across modes and completed sessions are saved automatically for review. Three optional network features—map tiles, reverse geocoding and weather—are separately gated and off by default; the policy says requests can reveal tile coordinates or session location/time and IP address to the respective provider. Source code is MIT and the exact bundled trained weights are declared Apache-2.0 in separate files at v1.2.1. This is a strong local-first field-recording and species-identification precedent, not evidence that an animal call has been translated or that the app understands a bird’s intent.
limitations: This is a documentation and release review, not an install, device test, packet capture, code audit or independent evaluation. The app classifies bird species; no evidence was reviewed here for identifying individual household parrots, call function or meaning. The model license does not clear training data, bundled images/taxonomy, dependencies or the BirdNET trademark. No training corpus was examined, and no Talk2Nature use or model transfer was tested. The official onboarding requires a microphone grant before the app is ready; this may be a poor fit for a first visit by a curious beginner. Local session auto-save and optional third-party location/weather requests need distinct user disclosure. This note does not independently verify the developer’s privacy statements or model-accuracy claims.
lesson: Separate a no-microphone learning exercise from actual observation and any species-classification feature. BirdNET Live demonstrates a mature local-first pattern: visible session review, explicit exports and deletion, model and code licenses tracked separately, and optional network integrations with individual controls. For Talk2Nature, keep the existing invented-scene practice easy to reach before asking for microphone access. Do not add BirdNET or another predictor to the observation flow until the intended species/task, model terms, runtime behavior, privacy, and held-out evaluation are reviewed. Species identification is not a statement about call meaning.
next_review: If considering a BirdNET model integration, pin and inspect the exact current app/model release, separately review model/data/asset terms and expected-species coverage, and evaluate on consented, independently labeled, grouped recordings from the intended context. Independently verify actual network behavior and deletion/export on supported devices. No audio, code or model acquisition is authorized by this note.

title: Island parakeet contact calls vary across locations
seo_description: A public brown-throated parakeet dataset pairs contact-call audio with acoustic measurements; it studies variation, not call meaning.
review_stage: Targeted publisher-indexed primary-article passages and the official Dryad v4 record/file manifest reviewed; no article or dataset file acquired.
review_depth: Reviewed the publisher-indexed abstract, recording approach, Table 1 location statement, frequency/SPCC-PCO methods, duration results and selected discussion passages; this is targeted review, not a complete article audit. The official Dryad API v2 record identifies dataset 77790, version 4 / version ID 147704, dates, dataset-level CC0-1.0 and eight file records with declared SHA-256 digests. The direct publisher fetch returned HTTP 403. The official README API download returned HTTP 401 and its record-page download link returned HTTP 403. No article PDF, README, spreadsheet, audio, supplement or code was acquired; upstream hashes were not locally checked.
finding: The study analyzes one call type, loud contact calls, rather than the species’ full vocal repertoire. It reports population-level differences in call duration, frequency measures and spectrogram structure/variability across five island populations and mainland Venezuela. The authors explicitly say receiver experiments are needed to test whether these acoustic patterns correspond to receiver responses. This is a useful parrot-specific acoustic-variation study, not a call-meaning or translation result.
limitations: Only selected article sections and public metadata were reviewed. The duration-results prose reports 1,319 calls from 92 units, while the 10 rows in Table 5 sum to 1,313 calls from 91 units; the article page does not reconcile this six-call/one-unit difference. Verify against the README and data before replication. The Dryad manifest contains no executable code file although the paper describes a custom MATLAB routine; no separate code repository was audited. Caller/group/session linkage, label provenance, recording conditions, exact mainland site rows, site sensitivity, split structure and receiver-response labels remain unverified. The article-specific reuse license was not established; the dataset-level CC0 record does not license the paper or a derived model. No qualified independent specialist review has occurred.
lesson: The most defensible first parrot task suggested by this source is a descriptive, group-aware replication of acoustic variation—not a system that translates a parrot. Keep call structure, population/site association, independently observed behavior and receiver response as different evidence levels. Even a reproducible classifier of island or caller labels would not establish what a call means.
